## INTRODUCTION

<meta>This page transitions from the general front matter into the formal editorial introduction, explaining the history and physical state of Leonardo's anatomical drawings in the Windsor collection and the methodology used to reconstruct the original notebooks.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION

This volume is the second in the publication of the Leonardo da Vinci manuscripts from the Royal Library of Windsor, a project initiated by Mr. Theodore Sabachnikoff. <note>Teodoro (Theodore) Sabachnikoff was a Russian scholar and collector who funded these early, high-quality facsimile editions of Leonardo's work.</note>

The rules established for us in the previous publications (**The Flight of Birds** and **Anatomy A**) will be strictly observed in this volume and in the series of volumes that will follow.

First, we will address the assembly of the book. It does not exist as a bound collection—as we present it here—nor is it in the original order in which Leonardo wrote it.

The entire treasure of the Leonardo collection at Windsor Castle consists of individual sheets that originally formed specific notebooks. However, over time—and even before they arrived at the Royal Library—these sheets were detached and scattered. Among these fragments, we are attempting to reconstruct the original books as far as possible.

Identifying the sheets that originally formed a single unit is not a grave difficulty, thanks to various physical clues such as the dimensions, the paper type, the ink, the tint, the handwriting, the presence of stains, and the alignment of <term>stitch marks|the physical holes left from where the papers were once sewn into a binding</term>. However, establishing the exact order in which they were written is often impossible due to missing pages, the discontinuity of subjects, and a total lack of original page numbering.

In this second volume of Anatomy—the sheets of which we have labeled with the letter **B** to distinguish it from the first (**Sheets A**) and the subsequent volumes reconstructed from the Royal Library papers—43 sheets remain.

<summary>This introduction describes the editorial process of reconstructing Leonardo da Vinci's anatomical notebooks from the dispersed collection at Windsor Castle, noting the physical evidence used to group the pages.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Royal Library of Windsor, Theodore Sabachnikoff, Anatomy B, manuscript reconstruction, codicology, anatomical drawings</keywords>

This volume is the second in the publication (initiated by
Mr. Theodore Sabachnikoff) of the manuscripts of Leonardo da Vinci, which
are held in the Royal Library at Windsor.

The rules that we imposed upon ourselves in the previous publications
(**The Flight of Birds** and **Anatomy A**), will be strictly
followed in this one and in the series of volumes that will follow it.

Thus, we will first proceed with the formation of the book; which exists
neither as a single collection, such as we are presenting it, nor in the order established by Leonardo
while writing it.

The entire treasure of the Leonardian collection at Windsor Castle con-
sists of sheets which, originally, formed specific books,
but they were detached and dispersed over time, and long before
reaching the Royal Library. We are attempting to reconstitute, as much
as is possible, the original books by means of these sheets.

The selection of sheets, which formed a whole originally, using
several physical indicators—such as dimensions, paper,
ink, tint, handwriting, stains, and the alignment of
sewing marks—does not present very great difficulties; but what is
often impossible is to positively establish the order of the leaves, either
because several are missing, or because of the discontinuity of the arguments
and the absence of numbering.

Of this second volume of Anatomy, for which we mark the sheets
with the letter **B**, to distinguish it from the first (**Sheets A**) and from
those following, reconstructed by us using the sheets from the Royal Library.

# INTRODUCTION

...undoubtedly forming, along with others, an originally complete book, which was probably written by Leonardo in 1489 ⁽¹⁾.

Of these 43 sheets, five—as we will indicate in the appropriate place—have the *recto* and *verso* <note>the front and back of a leaf</note> blank, and one (both *recto* and *verso*) deals exclusively with reproductive organs and functions; therefore, it will form part of Leonardo’s book on generation, which likewise belongs to the Royal Library at Windsor.

There are, therefore, 79 original pages published here, containing 193 figures in addition to the writings.

We provide a heliotype reproduction <note>an early photographic printing process using gelatin to create high-quality prints</note> of these pages in their original size and in an order that—based on many minutely studied clues—almost always coincides with the one established by Leonardo.

In this regard, we must note that some sheets are marked with ancient letters, and some with ancient and modern numbers; to be precise, we have recorded these marks in square brackets because they are not in Leonardo’s hand. However, they do not serve at all as a guide for the pagination.

The diplomatic transcription <term>diplomatic transcription: a precise, letter-for-letter copy of the original text, preserving all original spelling, abbreviations, and punctuation</term> therefore records, as we have stated previously, everything the original manuscript contains with the utmost accuracy; in essence, it is nothing more than *a second reproduction of the manuscript in typographic characters accessible to everyone* ⁽²⁾.

To this corresponds the explanatory critical transcription, which scrupulously maintains the integrity of the writing, changing only certain incidental details where such changes are necessary for a proper understanding.

The first transcription makes the text *readable*; the second makes it *understandable* ⁽³⁾.

Alongside these two transcriptions is the French translation, intended to bring the manifestations of Leonardo’s genius within reach of a greater number of scholars.

# INTRODUCTION

At the Royal Library, there remain 43 sheets, which originally certainly formed a complete book with the others, likely written by Leonardo in 1489 <note>original: "1489". Leonardo often dated his notebooks, providing a rare chronological anchor for his anatomical studies.</note> ^(1).

Of these 43 sheets, five—as we shall indicate in the appropriate place—have the *recto* <note>The front side of a leaf</note> and the *verso* <note>The back side of a leaf</note> blank, and one (*recto* and *verso*) deals exclusively with the organs and functions of generation <note>Reproduction and the reproductive system</note>, and consequently will form part of Leonardo’s book on generation, also belonging to the Royal Library at Windsor.

The original pages that we are now publishing therefore number 79, and they contain, along with the text, 193 figures.

We provide the heliotype <note>An early photographic process used for high-quality reproductions of manuscripts</note> reproduction of these pages, in the size of the original, and in the order which, according to several minutely studied clues, almost always coincides with that established by Leonardo.

We must note in this regard that some sheets are marked with ancient letters, and others by ancient and modern numbers—marks reported by us, for the sake of precision, within square brackets, because they are not in Leonardo’s hand; however, they do not serve as a guide for the layout.

The diplomatic transcription <note>A precise transcription that preserves the original spelling, punctuation, and layout exactly as written</note> then provides, as we have said before, with the greatest accuracy, everything contained in the original manuscript; it is, in substance, nothing but a *second reproduction of the manuscript in typographic characters accessible to all* ^(2).

To this transcription corresponds the explanatory critique, which scrupulously preserves the integrity of the text, changing only a few incidentals, the modification of which is indispensable to make it entirely intelligible.

The first transcription makes the text *readable*, the second makes it *understandable* ^(3).

To these two transcriptions corresponds the English translation <note>original: "traduction française". This refers to the French translation provided in the source volume this text introduces.</note>, to bring the manifestations of Leonardo's genius within reach of the greatest number of people.

(2, 3) Codex on the Flight of Birds, published by Th. Sabachnikoff. Transcriptions and notes by G. Piumati, pages 40-42.

# INTRODUCTION

In the margin, in their proper places, we provide the summaries of the writings and the figures.

Therefore, for each volume, according to the science it treats, we turn to the help of a specialist. For the first (**Anatomy - Sheets A**) we received valuable assistance from Doctor Antonio Dionisi of Rome; for the present one, we are very grateful for the cooperation of Doctor Adolfo Villa of the Surgical Clinic of the University of Turin.

We shall not discourse upon the importance of the present volume. Leonardo predates his time by centuries, revealing unexpected wonders to the scholar ⁽⁴⁾.

Nor is the profound and subtle diligence of study, which appears here in the marvelous drawings and anatomical writings, restricted to this science alone. To all of us—who by intellectual necessity and the immense, ever-growing breadth of the scientific field are forced within the limits of a specialized study—the universality of his genius awakens an ineffable sense of admiration and astonishment. While he paints and models the most marvelous works that art can boast, sufficient to fill and celebrate the life of one man, he simultaneously—and with equal mastery—studies and writes of painting, architecture, philosophy, physics, chemistry, astronomy, mechanics, hydraulics, geology, geography, botany, zoology... and not superficially, not vaguely, but entering into diligent research, revealing new, profound laws and minute details, in addition to the anatomy we are currently publishing.

Of all this immense labor, incomprehensible within the short span of an active life such as Leonardo’s, various volumes have already been published; namely: six large volumes of the Manuscripts existing at the Institute of France, by

(4) We cite, for example: the studies and drawings of myology <note>The study of the muscular system</note> and osteology <note>The study of the structure and function of bones</note>, the comparisons of man with the monkey (Fol. 9 verso, page 63), the chapter "On the muscles that move the tongue" (Fol. 28 verso, page 173 and following) where, passing from the anatomical field to the physiological, and then to the philological <note>The study of language in oral and written historical sources</note> and idealistic, he gives us a wonderful page of thoughts and *modern* philosophy; and we further note the study on the crossing of the visual nerves (Fol. 35 recto, page 215).

# INTRODUCTION

In the margin, in their proper places, we provide the summaries <note>original: "arguments"</note> of the writings and the figures.

To this end, and for each volume, according to the branch of science it treats, we have recourse to the help of a specialized scholar. For the first (**Anatomy - Sheets A**), we were valiantly assisted by Doctor Antonio Dionisi of Rome; for the present volume, we express our gratitude to Doctor Adolfo Villa, of the Surgical Clinic of the University of Turin.

We shall not speak here of the importance of the present volume. Leonardo is centuries ahead of his time, revealing unexpected wonders to those who study him ⁽⁴⁾.

The profound and subtle diligence of study, which appears here in these marvelous drawings and anatomical writings, is not limited to this science alone. The universality of his genius evokes an ineffable feeling of admiration and astonishment in all of us, whom the necessities of intellect and the ever-growing breadth of the scientific field constrain within the limits of specialized studies. While he paints and models the most marvelous works that honor the arts—sufficient in themselves to fill and make famous the life of one man—as the valiant soul he is, he also studies and writes (besides the Anatomy we are publishing) on painting, architecture, philosophy, physics, chemistry, astronomy, mechanics, hydraulics, geology, geography, botany, and zoology... not superficially, nor vaguely, but by engaging in diligent research and revealing new and profound laws, as well as minute details.

Of all this enormous labor, incomprehensible within the short span of a life as active as Leonardo’s, several volumes have already been published; namely: six large volumes of the Manuscripts that exist at the <note>This likely refers to the Institut de France in Paris, where many of Leonardo's notebooks are held.</note>

---

(4) Let us recall, for example, the studies and drawings of <term>myology|The study of the muscular system</term> and <term>osteology|The study of the skeletal system</term>, the comparisons between man and monkey (Folio 9 verso, page 63), the chapter: “Of the muscles that move the tongue” (Folio 28 verso, page 173 and following) where, passing from the anatomical field to the physiological, and then to <term>philology|The study of language and historical texts</term> and idealism, he gives us an admirable page of thought and *modern* philosophy; let us also recall the study on the crossing of the visual nerves <note>This refers to the optic chiasm, where the optic nerves cross.</note> (Folio 35 recto, page 215).

# INTRODUCTION

Charles Ravaisson-Mollien; the *Trivulzio Codex*, by Luca Beltrami; the *Codex on the Flight of Birds* and *Anatomy A*, by Teodoro Sabachnikoff; and the great *Codex Atlanticus* is currently in press, of which approximately one thousand large folio pages and 920 heliotype plates—reproducing over 1200 originals—have already been released ⁽⁵⁾.

And there remain unpublished sheets scattered here and there, the continuation of the great collection of the Royal Library at Windsor, the volumes of the British Museum and the South Kensington Museum <note>Now the Victoria and Albert Museum</note> in London, a complex of over 1500 pages!

The publication of this scientific treasure was promised by Teodoro Sabachnikoff in his preface to the *Codex on the Flight of Birds* ⁽⁶⁾, and the promise will be kept. The other volumes of the Windsor manuscripts will follow the present one, and, simultaneously or after them, those of the British Museum and the South Kensington Museum.

->Turin, August 1901.<-

->G. PIUMATI.<-

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

<margin>
and their functional dependence on this [the common sense] in the individual under normal conditions:

Sight.
</margin>

...which is called the **common sense** <note>original: "senso comune"; in Renaissance anatomy, this was the central faculty of the brain where all senses were thought to meet</note>. And it is not distributed throughout the entire body, as many have believed; rather, it is entirely in one part. For if it were distributed throughout, and entirely in every part, it would not have been necessary for the instruments of the senses to converge at one single place. Instead, it would have sufficed for the eye to perform its sensory function upon its own surface, rather than sending the <term>similitude</term> <note>the "species" or visual image of an object</note> of the things seen to the [central] sense via the optic nerves; for the soul, by the reasoning mentioned above, could have perceived them right there upon the surface of the eye.

<margin>Hearing.</margin>

And similarly for the sense of hearing; it would have sufficed merely for the voice to resonate within the hollow pores of the **petrous bone** <note>the hard part of the temporal bone containing the inner ear</note> located inside the ear, without creating another passage from that bone to the common sense, through which that "voice" must travel to the common judgment.

<margin>Smell.</margin>

The sense of smell is also seen to be constrained by necessity to converge at the said judgment. <insert>Taste and touch</insert>

---

<margin>
and their functional dependence on this in the individual under normal conditions:

Sight.
</margin>

...is called the common sense; and it is not all through the whole body, as many have believed; rather, it is all in that part; because, if it were all through the whole, and all in every part, it would not be necessary to make the instruments of the senses converge among themselves to a single place; rather, it would suffice that the eye performed the office of feeling on its surface, and not send, by way of the optic nerves, the likeness of the things seen to the sense; for the soul, for the reason said above, could understand them on that surface of the eye.

<margin>Hearing.</margin>

And likewise the sense of hearing; it would suffice only that the voice resonated in the concave porosities of the petrous bone, which is inside the ear, and not make from that bone to the common sense another transit, where that mouth <note>metaphor for the opening/conduit of the sense</note> has to run to the common judgment.

<margin>Smell.</margin>

The sense of smell, too, is seen to be forced by necessity to converge at the said judgment. (*Taste and touch*)

<summary>Leonardo argues that the "common sense" (the soul's seat) must be located in a specific part of the brain rather than diffused throughout the body, using the anatomical convergence of nerves as evidence. He reasons that if the soul were everywhere, sensory organs wouldn't need complex neural pathways to transmit data to a central point.</summary>
<keywords>common sense, anatomy, optic nerves, petrous bone, sensory perception, soul, Leonardo da Vinci, physiology</keywords>

# ON ANATOMY — FOLIO B — 2 RECTO

<margin>Touch.</margin>
Touch itself does not pass through the hollow cords <note>original: "chorde forate"; Leonardo often used the term "cords" to refer to nerves, which he believed were hollow tubes through which "animal spirits" or sensory information flowed</note>, but is carried to that sense [the common sense] by cords that spread out with infinite branching into the skin, which surrounds the bodily limbs and internal organs.

(The nerves) The perforating cords carry the command and the feeling to the <term>functional organs</term> <note>original: "membri ofitialj"; literally "official members," referring to body parts that perform a specific duty or movement</note>. These cords, having entered among the muscles and <term>tendons</term> <note>original: "laciertj"; a term used in Renaissance anatomy to describe the fibrous, fleshy parts of muscles or the tendons themselves</note>, command them to move, and they obey. This obedience is put into action through swelling; for the swelling shortens their length and pulls back the nerves which are woven through the particles of the limbs. Being infused into the tips of the fingers, they carry to the sense the cause of their contact.

The nerves, with their muscles, serve the cords as soldiers serve their commanders; and the cords serve the **common sense** <note>the central faculty of the brain where all sensory inputs are processed</note> as commanders serve a captain; and the common sense serves the **soul** as the captain serves his lord.

<summary>Leonardo describes the nervous system's role in the sense of touch and muscle contraction, using a military hierarchy to illustrate how physical movement is commanded by the soul via the "common sense."</summary>
<keywords>touch, nerves, muscles, common sense, soul, anatomy, physiology, motor control</keywords>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

(Therefore, the nerve serves the muscle, and the muscle—)

Therefore, the **joint of the bones** obeys the nerve, and the nerve the muscle, and the muscle the cord <note>original: "chorda"; here Leonardo refers to the tendon or the fibrous part of the muscle that transmits force</note>, and the cord obeys the **common sense** <note>the central hub in the brain where Leonardo believed all senses were coordinated</note>, and the common sense is the **seat of the soul**. Memory is its <term>storehouse</term> <note>original: "ammunizione"; literally "munitions" or "provisions," suggesting memory is where the soul's materials are kept</note>, and the <term>perceptive faculty</term> <note>original: "imprensiva"; Leonardo's term for the specific part of the brain that receives and "impresses" sensory data</note> is its secretary <note>original: "referendaria"; an official who reports information to a higher authority</note>, (and the heart is its...).

Just as the senses give to the soul, and not the soul to the senses; so, where the sense—which is the official of the soul—is missing, the soul in this life lacks any knowledge of the function of that sense. This is clearly seen in the case of one born mute or born blind.

<margin>
Why the muscles of the heart are thicker toward the base than toward the apex <note>The 'apex' refers to the pointed bottom tip of the heart.</note>.
</margin>

That part of the heart which is closer to the base shall be of a thicker and harder substance than that which is closer to its apex; and this happens because the muscles that move the valves of the heart have their root and origin in said base, and because the base is that which receives and sustains the percussion <note>The forceful impact or pressure</note> of the blood that swells within its ventricles.

**On the nature of the muscles that close the doors <note>Leonardo uses 'porte' (doors) to describe the heart valves.</note> of the heart.**
The muscles that close the doors of the heart are of the nature of sinew and cord; and this is done by Nature so that such muscles do not have to stretch, but rather to resist the force of the blood which would seek to push them back into the ventricles from whence it came.

<margin>
Why the sinews <note>original: "nervi" - in this context, Leonardo refers to the chordae tendineae or tendons rather than the modern neurological 'nerve'.</note> of the heart are not elastic.
</margin>

Whether the power of the heart's expansion is equal to the power of its constriction.

These and many other reasons will be treated in their proper place; and first we shall define the nature of the muscles, the sinews, and the cords, and how the muscles are born from the sinews and how the cords are converted into muscles, and then how the sinews, muscles, and cords move the limbs...

<margin>
On the motion of the blood.
</margin>

The blood that enters with impetus into the ventricles of the heart strikes against the valves and closes them, and at the same time opens the valves that provide the exit for the blood that was already in the ventricle...

the method of the well of San Lorenzo
of the hill of San Lorenzo <note>Likely referring to the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Florence or a specific engineering project nearby.</note>

The principle of weights that move upon wheels is that one must give so much force to that wheel that one of its sides is equal to the other; and thus it will move along its path as is seen in the weights of a balance, which, being equal, move through the motion with the force of the air that moves them or by some other accidental motion.

If you want to see how the weight of the wheel is equal on one side and the other—if you want to see the <term>weight</term> <note>original: "p'o" (abbreviation for peso)</note> of that wheel that must turn—place the <term>axle</term> <note>original: "uita" (literally 'screw', here meaning the central axis)</note> of the center of said wheel upon two <term>pivots</term> <note>original: "bilichi" (supports or bearings)</note> of steel, well-joined and polished; and then you shall give a turn to said wheel, and if it stops near the place where it began that motion, the weight is equal. And if it stops from time to time in various places, it is more perfectly equal. And if said wheel always stops in one place, that place is the heaviest; and if it always stops with that place at the bottom, that is the [heaviest] weight of said wheel.

Furthermore, if you want to know how much weight is required to move said wheel with all its heaviness, put a weight on the pivot of its sides and watch what weight is needed to make it move; and that will be the force it will have to move in every one of its motions.

If you want to see how the weight of said wheel is equal above and below, make it so that said wheel is turned flat like a grindstone, and place the axle of its center upon a sharp pivot; and if said wheel hangs more to one side than the other, that side is the heaviest.

Furthermore, if you want to know if said wheel is heavier in one of its turns than in another, place said wheel with its axle inside a hole equal to said axle; and if it turns easily, the side that lowers itself is the heaviest.

The principle of weights that move upon wheels is that one must give so much force to that wheel that one of its sides is equal to the other.

# On the Motion of Weights and the Nature of the Balance

The center of the weight of any body whatsoever is that which divides it into two equal parts, in such a way that one part is as heavy as the other. <note>Leonardo is defining the center of gravity here, a concept central to his mechanical studies.</note>

### Of the Balance

The balance is a <term>mechanical instrument</term> <note>original: "strumento di silio" (likely a reference to 'Sillio' or a corruption of 'mechanics')</note> which is composed of a beam and a fulcrum. And that part of the beam which is between the fulcrum and the end where the weight is placed is called the arm of the balance.

<column-break/>

->**The Experiment of the Cord**<-

If a cord is wound around a wheel, and to the end of this cord a weight is attached, this weight will move the wheel with more or less force according to the distance that the cord is from the center of the wheel. 

<margin>
The weight that descends 
moves the weight 
that ascends.
</margin>

Every weight desires to fall toward the center of the world by the shortest way. <note>Leonardo often uses "center of the world" to refer to the center of the Earth, following the Aristotelian view of gravity.</note> If a weight is placed upon a slanted plane, it will move toward the lowest part of that plane, provided that the friction of the plane does not resist it.

### Observations on Water

<insert>Water does not move of itself unless it descends.</insert>

The water that falls from a height of one <term>braccio</term> <note>A Florentine measure of length, approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> has the same force as the water that falls from two <term>braccia</term> if the quantity of the second is half of the first.

| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| 2 Braccia | 1 Measure | Equal Force |
<table-end>

Note the

of the 
impact.
</margin>

How the nerves sometimes operate by themselves, without the command of the other <term>officials</term> <note>Leonardo uses the term "ofitialj" (officials) to describe the various organs and faculties of the body as if they were workers in a government or household.</note> and of the soul.

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

<margin>Function of the bile.</margin>
The <term>gall</term> <note>original: "fiele," referring to bile or the gallbladder</note> is the servant or attendant of the liver; it sweeps and cleans away all the impurities and leftover waste of the nourishment that has been distributed to the limbs by the liver.

<margin>Intestines.</margin>
[Fig. 5.]
[Fig. 6.]

You will understand their winding paths well if you inflate them. And remember that once you have drawn them from four perspectives in their natural arrangement, you should then draw them from four other perspectives spread apart, so that through the spaces and openings between them, you can understand the whole—that is, the variations in their thickness.

<margin>On the erection in relation to the increased flow of blood to the penis.</margin>
Concerning the <term>virile member</term> <note>the penis</note>: when it is hard, it is large, long, dense, and heavy. And when it is <insert>soft</insert> <note>original: "tenero," literally tender or soft</note>, thin, short, and limp—that is, weak. One must judge that neither flesh nor "wind" <note>Leonardo is refuting the ancient Greek theory that erections were caused by air or "pneuma" (wind) inflating the organ.</note> is added here, but rather arterial blood. I have seen this in the dead who have this member erect, for many die in this state—especially those who have been hanged, whom I have observed.

<summary>Leonardo identifies bile as a cleansing agent for the body's digestive waste and provides a methodology for anatomical drawing using inflation and multiple perspectives. The longer a crossbow bolt is, and of equal thickness, the more powerful its impact will be; because as the bolt leaves the string of that crossbow, the motion remains straight until the end of its travel. This is because the air, which is directly in front of the bolt, offers the greatest resistance; a bolt that is short and of equal thickness is more easily turned <note>original: "uoltarzj," referring to tumbling or wobbling in flight</note> by the air, and because of this turning, the air offers it maximum resistance. Consequently, such a bolt loses the force of its motion in a short distance. But if the bolt is long and of equal thickness, it is easier for it to "break" <note>original: "rompello," meaning to pierce or cut through</note> the air directly, and for this reason, such a bolt maintains its motion for a long distance, and therefore its impact is that much more powerful.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes why long, straight crossbow bolts are more effective than short ones, concluding that their length prevents tumbling and allows them to pierce air resistance more efficiently. He also compares this to the internal pressure of flowing water, which is strongest in the center where it cannot escape laterally.</summary>

### ON ANATOMY — FOLIO B — 3 RECTO

->FOLIO 3 — recto. [14 3.]<-

<margin>Long nails among the Europeans and the Indians.</margin>
Long nails among the Europeans are considered shameful, but among the Indians they are held in great veneration. They have them painted with penetrating liquids and adorn them with various perforations; they say that this is a mark of noblemen, and that short nails are for laborers and mechanics in various trades.

<margin>Function of the chyliferous system.</margin>
Through the branching of the chyle vein <note>original: "vena del chilo"; refers to the lacteal vessels that transport chyle, a milky fluid containing fats, from the intestines</note> in the mesentery, nourishment is drawn from the breakdown <note>original: "corruttione", here meaning the metabolic breakdown or "corruption" of food into nutrients</note> of food in the intestines. Ultimately, it returns through the extreme branches of the artery to those intestines where, the blood then being "dead," it decomposes and acquires that stench characteristic of feces.

[Fig. 7.]

<margin>Veins of the peritoneum and the mesentery.</margin>
*b c* is the vein that nourishes the omentum <note>original: "zirbo", an archaic term for the omentum or epiploon, the fatty tissue covering the abdominal organs</note>, and it is located in front of the vein *a n*, which is the one that nourishes the mesentery; between the mesentery and the omentum, the intestines are enclosed.

<column-break/>

->FOLIO 3 — recto. [14 3.]<-

<margin>Long nails among the Europeans and the Indians.</margin>
Long nails among the Europeans are considered shameful, and among the Indians they are held in great veneration; they have them painted with penetrating liquids, and they adorn them with different perforations, and they say that this suits gentlemen, and that short nails are the property of workers and mechanics in various trades.

<margin>Function of the chyle system.</margin>
By the branching of the chyle vein in the mesentery <note>mesentery: the fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and holds them in place</note>, the nourishment is drawn from the breakdown of food in the intestines, and lastly it returns, through the extreme ramifications of the artery, to these intestines, where this blood then being dead, it corrupts, and it takes on that stench that excrement smells of.

[Fig. 7.]

*b c* is the vein that nourishes the omentum, and it remains in front of the vein *a n*, which is that which nourishes the mesentery, and between the mesentery and the omentum the intestines are contained.

### FOLIO 3 — verso. [205 [?]]
#### on the force of the muscles

<margin>The skin is the cause of the strength of the arms and legs.</margin>
If any muscle is pulled lengthwise, a small force breaks its fleshiness; and if the <term>nerves of sensation</term> <note>original: "nervi del sentimento"; Leonardo refers to the nerves that carry both feeling and the "animal spirits" believed to trigger movement</note> are pulled lengthwise, a small power plucks them from the muscles where their branching is woven, spread, and consumed; and the same is seen to happen to the fibrous <term>sheath</term> <note>original: "vesta," literally "garment" or "clothing"</note> of the veins and arteries that are mixed with these muscles. What then is the cause of such great strength in the arms or legs, as is seen in the actions of any animal? Nothing else can be said than that it is the skin that clothes them; which, because the nerves of sensation thicken the muscles, and these muscles shorten and pull the <term>cords</term> <note>original: "corde"; Leonardo's term for tendons</note> behind them into which their ends are converted; and in such thickening they fill the skin and make it taut and hard; and it cannot be stretched unless the muscles thin out; and, by not thinning, they are the cause of resistance and of making the aforesaid skin strong, in which the enlarged muscles perform the function of a <term>wedge</term> <note>original: "conio"; Leonardo uses a mechanical analogy where the muscle acting against the container of the skin creates a mechanical advantage.</note>.

---

-># On the function of the nerves<-

The branches of the nerves are of two natures, of which one part goes to the sensory muscles <note>original: "muscoli sentitivi"</note> and the other to the motor muscles <note>original: "muscoli movitivi"</note>; and one part goes to the exterior muscles and the other to the interior muscles; and among these interior muscles there is another subdivision, because some are of voluntary movements and others of involuntary movements. The muscles of voluntary movements are those that are exercised by the will, and the muscles of involuntary movements are those that move by themselves, such as the heart and the lungs and the diaphragm and the liver and the stomach and the spleen and the intestines; but the diaphragm is that which more than any other is of a mixed nature, because it is that which is largely obedient to the will and in part is involuntary, as happens in laughter and in hiccuping and in sneezing and in other similar acts.

<note>Anatomical study of the brachial plexus and rib cage</note>

<margin>

All the nerves that have to give motion to the limbs join together in the chest and from there they divide to the limbs. But those that have to give sensation to the senses are divided from one another from their very origin. And this happens because motion is made by the force of the contraction <note>original: "contraffazione," referring here to the mechanical shortening or tightening of the muscle fibers</note> of muscles, which muscles cannot perform their function <term>ufitio (office/function): the specific physiological role or duty of a body part</term> if they are not pulled by the nerves; and because many muscles must concur in one and the same movement, it is necessary that their nerves join together in one and the same place, as is seen in this drawing.

<note>The bottom right section contains schematic diagrams of the spinal column and the branching of nerve roots.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the brachial plexus, distinguishing between sensory and motor nerves while identifying the diaphragm as a unique muscle controlled by both voluntary and involuntary impulses. He concludes that motor nerves must converge into networks to coordinate the complex contractions of multiple muscles for a single movement.</summary>

-># On the function of the nerves<-

The branches of the nerves are of two natures, of which one part goes to the **sensory muscles** <note>original: "muscoli sentitivi"; those responsible for feeling</note> and the other to the **motor muscles** <note>original: "muscoli movitivi"; those responsible for movement</note>; and one part goes to the exterior muscles and the other to the interior muscles; and among these interior muscles there is another subdivision, because some are of voluntary movements and others of involuntary movements. The muscles of voluntary movements are those that are exercised by the will, and the muscles of involuntary movements are those that move by themselves, such as the heart and the lungs and the diaphragm and the liver and the stomach and the spleen and the intestines; but the diaphragm is that which more than any other is of a mixed nature, because it is that which is largely obedient to the will and in part is involuntary, as happens in laughter and in hiccuping and in sneezing and in other similar acts.

# ON ANATOMY. — FOLIO B. — 5 RECTO.

->FOLIO 5 — *recto*. [3 38]<-

<margin>
Femoral nerve,
sciatic nerve,
and veins
of the lower
limb.
</margin>
[Fig. 22 :] nerve of the leg bone <note>original: "neruo fucile"; "fucile" (literally 'flint' or 'steel') was an anatomical term used by Leonardo to refer to the long bones of the arm or leg, in this case, likely the fibula or tibia.</note>
[Fig. 23 :] external nerve (vein) of the leg bone <note>original: "siluesstre focile"; Leonardo uses "silvestre" (wild) to denote superficial or external structures and "domestiche" (domestic) for internal ones.</note>
[Fig. 24 :] internal veins, and from the knee downward they become external.

<margin>
Reason
for the position
of the veins
in the knee.
</margin>
Nature has placed the <term>main veins</term> <note>original: "ueue maestre"; the primary vessels responsible for major blood flow.</note> of the leg in the middle of the thickness of the knee joint, because in the bending of that joint, the veins are less compressed than they would be if they passed in front of or behind the knee.

<margin>
Relationship
of the nerves
with the muscles.
</margin>
There are as many branches of the nerves as there are muscles, and there can be neither more nor fewer, because these muscles only contract or extend because of these nerves, from which the muscles receive their sensation. And there are as many motor cords <note>referring to the functional "pull" or tendons of the muscle</note> of the limbs as there are muscles.

<summary>Leonardo observes that nature places major veins in the center of the knee joint to protect them from being pinched during movement, and he asserts a direct proportional relationship between nerves and the muscles they control.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, knee joint, vascular system, nervous system, muscle contraction, physiology, leg veins</keywords>

Note why nature has placed so many branches of vessels in this place, as you see: <note>original: "nota perche la natura à mèsso tanti e rami uasi ĩ questo locho come tu uedi"</note> because if she <note>Leonardo frequently personifies Nature as a wise designer or engineer.</note> had wished to make just one, it <unclear>would be</unclear> too thick and could not <unclear>bend</unclear>; <note>original: "perche se li uolessi fare uno solo esso sarebe tropo grosso e nõ si potrebbe piegare"</note> and also because small branches <unclear>are more</unclear> suited to provide nourishment to the <unclear>muscles</unclear> <unclear>that are underneath</unclear>. <note>original: "e achora perche li rami piccoli sono più disposti a dare il nutrimento alli muscoli che s'è sotto"</note>

<note>Leonardo is applying a mechanical principle here: a single thick cable or "vessel" would impede the movement of the ankle and knee, whereas a network of fine "branches" allows for flexibility while efficiently distributing blood (or "nourishment") to the surrounding tissues.</note>

<summary>Leonardo illustrates the vascular or nervous system of the leg, arguing that nature uses many small branches instead of one large vessel to ensure limb flexibility and better nutrient distribution.</summary>

# Anatomical Studies of the Shoulder

<margin>
All the tendons <note>original: "nervi"; Leonardo often used this term to describe tendons, ligaments, or muscles interchangeably</note> of the shoulder are placed in a position beneath the head <note>original: "capello," literally "hat" or "cap"</note> of the humerus <note>the long bone of the upper arm</note>, which humerus performs the function of a pivot.
</margin>

<margin>
And in this manner, the tendons of the head of the humerus act in order to lift [the arm].
</margin>

<margin>
The pivot is in the middle, between the weight and the power <note>original: "potentia"; referring to the force or muscular strength applied to the lever</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
Here the pivot is not in the middle, but is at one of the ends.
</margin>

<note>Leonardo is comparing the shoulder joint to different classes of levers. In his diagrams, he explores how the placement of the "pivolo" (fulcrum) relative to the "potentia" (muscle force) and "peso" (the weight of the arm) changes the mechanical advantage of the limb.</note>

<column-break/>

<note>The following terms represent the core vocabulary of Leonardo's mechanical-anatomical analysis on this page:</note>

*   **Tendons/Nerves** <note>original: "nervi"</note>
*   **Shoulder** <note>original: "spalla"</note>
*   **Humerus** <note>original: "omero"</note>
*   **Pivot/Fulcrum** <note>original: "pivolo"</note>
*   **Power/Force** <note>original: "potentia"</note>
*   **Weight** <note>original: "peso"</note>
*   **Head of the humerus** <note>original: "capello de l'omero"</note>

<summary>This page features Leonardo da Vinci's mechanical analysis of the shoulder joint, where he identifies the humerus as a pivot and the tendons as cords of force. He classifies the movement of the arm according to the physics of levers, distinguishing between systems where the fulcrum is central or at the extremity.</summary>

## 7 — Front (Continued)

<note>Leonardo often utilized a comparative method in his drawings, showing the same limb multiple times to isolate different biological systems—a technique still used in modern medical illustration.</note>

The middle nerve <note>likely referring to the sciatic nerve or its division into the tibial nerve</note> which divides among the muscles of the leg below the knee, extends through the leg in such a way that its branches mingle with the branches of the veins that spread through that same leg. This is shown in the illustration above: in the drawing of the middle leg, the nerve is seen with its branches arranged and mixed with the branches of the veins; in the drawing on the right, one sees the branches of those veins; and in the one on the left, one sees the branches of the nerves. The same pattern occurs in the feet; and you shall further summarize in this section all the veins, nerves, and arteries of the leg and foot.

The nerve divides among its branches.
</margin>

<note>Leonardo’s observation that nerves and vessels "mix" reflects his effort to map the "plumbing" of the body. He was particularly interested in how these systems reached the very ends of the body to provide both nourishment (blood) and sensation or movement (nerves).</note>

# ANATOMY — Studies of the Hand and Nervous System

Just as the nerve <note>Leonardo frequently used the Italian word "neruo" (nerve) to refer to both the nerves that transmit sensation and the tendons that physically move the limbs.</note> that is in the middle of the nerves that open the fingers of the hand is that which... the nerves that go to these fingers intertwine together; furthermore, the nerves that go to the fingers of the hand intertwine together as you see illustrated below. Nature does this so that each of these fingers can operate independently <note>Leonardo was fascinated by the "autonomy" of the fingers, seeking the mechanical reason why we can move one finger without moving the others.</note>.

<margin>
It will seem like an incredible thing to those who have not seen **anatomy** <note>original: "notomia"</note>, but observe how the nerves situated on the upper part of the **forearm** <note>original: "antibracchio"</note>—which pull the fingers toward the back of the hand and are called the **extensor** <note>original: "distenditori"</note> nerves of these fingers—[act] as if by themselves without being helped...
</margin>

***

### [Study of the Hand]

<note>Above the hand is a fainter, more conceptual sketch. It shows a branching system descending from the neck/head area, representing the spinal cord and the nerves that carry "animal spirits" (the Renaissance concept of neurological impulses) from the brain to the extremities.</note>

### Anatomical and Mechanical Observations

**16** <note>Annotation in mirror script near the top left skeletal sketch</note>
This sketch illustrates the articulation of the **humerus** <note>the upper arm bone</note>, **radius**, and **ulna** <note>the two bones of the forearm</note>. Leonardo depicts the human arm in a flexed position to study how the bones fit together during movement.

**47** <note>Annotation in mirror script near the top right skeletal sketch</note>

**48** <note>Annotation in mirror script near the vertical line sketch</note>
A minimalist sketch representing a line of tension. This likely represents a single <term>tendon</term> <note>Leonardo often used the word "corda" or "string" to describe tendons</note> or the curved profile of a muscle's action against the bone.

**49** <note>Annotation in mirror script near the geometric diagram</note>

This diagram serves as a geometric proof for the note in the margin, demonstrating how the foot acts as a lever to support the body's weight on tiptoe without causing excessive strain or <term>fatigue</term> <note>original: "faticcha"</note> to the calf muscle.

O observer of this machine of ours <note>Leonardo frequently referred to the human body as a "machina" (machine) to highlight the mechanical perfection of its biological systems.</note>, do not be saddened that you gain knowledge of it through the death of others; but rather rejoice that our Creator <note>original: "altore" — literally "author" or "nourisher," referring to God as the designer of nature.</note> has anchored the intellect to such an excellent instrument.

### FOLIO 10 — verso. [24 86 [?]]

<margin>
Senile alterations of the hepatic arteries and veins, and their consequences.

[Fig. 53.]

The artery and the vein, which in the elderly extend between the spleen and the liver, become of such thickness of skin <note>Leonardo uses "pelle" (skin) to refer to the tunica or wall of the blood vessels</note> that it closes off the passage of the blood that comes from the <term>mesaraic veins</term> <note>The mesenteric veins, which carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</note>, through which this blood flows to the liver and to the heart and to the two major veins, and, consequently, through the whole body. And such veins, beyond the thickening of the skin, increase in length and twist themselves in the manner of a snake. And the liver loses the <term>humor</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "humors" were the vital fluids of the body; here it refers to the nourishing blood</note> of the blood which was brought to it by these; whereby this liver dries up and becomes like frozen bran, both in color and in substance, so that with little friction applied to it, this matter falls away in tiny particles like sawdust, leaving the veins and arteries exposed. And the veins of the gall bladder and of the umbilicus, which entered into this liver through the <term>portal of the liver</term> <note>The porta hepatis, the gateway where vessels enter the organ</note>, remain entirely...

### ON ANATOMY — FOLIO B — 10 VERSO

...I found [death] to occur through the failure of blood and the artery which nourished the heart and the other lower members, which I found very withered, lean, and dry. This <term>dissection</term> <note>original: "notomja"</note> I described very diligently and with great ease, because he was devoid of fat and <term>humors</term> <note>Renaissance medical term for bodily fluids; Leonardo notes that the absence of these fluids and fat makes the internal structures much easier to see and map</note>, which greatly impede the knowledge of the parts. The other dissection was of a boy of 2 years, in whom I found everything to be the opposite of that of the old man.

<margin>
The elderly who live in health die through a lack of nourishment. This happens because the passage to the <term>mesenteric veins</term> <note>original: "vene mjseraice"; the veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</note> is continually restricted by the thickening of the walls <note>original: "pelle," literally "skin"</note> of these veins, progressing all the way to the capillary veins, which are the first to close up entirely. From this it arises that the elderly fear the cold more than the young, and that those who are very old have skin the color of wood or of a dry chestnut, because such skin is almost completely deprived of nourishment.
</margin>

And such a <term>tunic</term> <note>the "tunica" refers to the layers or walls of a blood vessel</note> of the veins acts in man as it does in oranges <note>original: "pomerancj"; likely referring to the thickening rind or the drying segments of the fruit</note>, in which the more...

# LEONARDO DA VINCI
## Page 24

-> [Illustration: A small pen-and-ink sketch by Leonardo da Vinci depicting a bird-like form with outstretched wings, capturing the essence of motion.] <-

If the air were of such thinness <note>original: "sottiglieza"—referring to low density or lack of substance</note> that it did not resist the motion of any thing that moved within it, the motion of that thing would have no impediment; and if the air were of such density that it did not yield to the motion of any thing, such a thing would not move through it. But the air is in such a state between the motion of a thing and the air itself, that it does not resist the motion of a thing so much that it cannot move through it, and yet it is not of such [low] density that it does not yield to the motion of a thing; wherefore the bird, which is heavier than the air, remains suspended by it and flies, and likewise the fish in the water and the worm in the earth.

---

<margin>
if the bird
did not move
so that it had
air before it and

wing had
impediment
because the wings beat
the air and make it
flee from under the wings
and this flight
of air is the cause
that the air which is under
the wing condenses <note>Leonardo uses "condēsi" to mean the compression or thickening of air under pressure.</note>
and creates resistance
to the weight of the bird
and supports it
</margin>

The bird would move its wing forward with a [certain] motion, and both one and the other [wing] would move without any impediment if it had air that yielded to it not without difficulty. But the air resists the motion of the wings, and the wings beat the air and make it flee from under the wings; and this flight of air is the reason that the air which is under the wing condenses and creates resistance to the weight of the bird and supports it, and the bird, through the resistance of the air, raises itself upward.

---

<margin>
the bird by
itself
supports itself
without beating
its wings and does not fall
to the ground if the air
does not yield to
its weight, and the air
does not yield to
its weight except
inasmuch as it [the air] was
resistant to it
</margin>

All things weigh as much as they weigh when not suspended by anything; but the air, being moved between the weight and the motion of the wings of a bird, resists the weight of that bird, and the bird, which is above that air, leans upon it with the resistance that the air makes to that bird. And it leans upon it all the more as the air is denser, and it leans upon it all the more as the bird is faster in its motion, because the faster the bird is, the more air it strikes, and the more it condenses it, and the more the air resists it.

<note>Leonardo investigates the physics of flight, theorizing that air resistance and the compression <term>condensazione: the act of making air more dense through pressure</term> of air beneath a bird's wings provide the lift necessary for flight. The text uses his characteristic mirror writing and abbreviations, such as tildes over vowels to indicate missing 'n' or 'm' sounds (e.g., "impedimēto" for "impedimento").</note>

**Glossary of terms used by Leonardo:**
<gloss>bird (uccello)</gloss>, <gloss>air (aria)</gloss>, <gloss>resistance (rēsistēza)</gloss>, <gloss>density (dēsità)</gloss>, <gloss>motion (moto)</gloss>, <gloss>wing (ala)</gloss>, <gloss>weight (peso)</gloss>, <gloss>condenses/compresses (condēsa)</gloss>

<summary>On this page, Leonardo da Vinci outlines a precocious theory of aerodynamics, explaining that flight is possible because air possesses a physical density that resists a bird's wings. He argues that the speed of a wing beat compresses the air beneath it, creating a solid enough "support" to counteract the bird's weight and provide lift.</summary>
<keywords>aerodynamics, bird flight, air resistance, compression of air, physics of motion, mechanics, weight and gravity</keywords>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

All the veins and arteries originate from the heart; and the reason is that the greatest thickness found in these veins and arteries is at the junction they have with the heart. And the further they move away from the heart, the more they thin out and divide into more minute ramifications. 

And if you were to say that the veins originate in the protuberance <term>protuberance: original "gibbosità," referring to the rounded lobes of the liver</term> of the liver because they have their ramifications in that protuberance—just as the roots of plants are in the earth—the answer to this comparison is that plants do not have their origin in their roots. Rather, the roots and the other ramifications have their origin from the lower part of these plants, which stands between the air and the earth. 

And all the parts of the plant, both lower and upper, are always smaller than that part which borders the earth. Therefore, it is manifest that the entire plant has its origin from that thickness, and consequently, the veins have their origin from the heart, where their greatest thickness is found. Nor is a plant ever found that has its origin from the <insert>tips of its roots or other branches.</insert> <margin>+ [Continued in the margin at the sign +:] tips of their roots or other branches.</margin>

<summary>Leonardo argues that the heart, not the liver, is the origin of the vascular system by comparing the thickness of blood vessels to the trunk of a tree, which is always thicker than its roots or branches.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, heart, veins, arteries, liver, botanical analogy, vascular system, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

Nature does not fail in anything; not even in giving motion to the lungs so that they do not press against one another, giving them the air and the spirit <note>original: "anima"</note> in a valley of supreme refreshment.

The lungs maintain the heart by not touching the flesh while it swells, so that the beats do not strike [the lungs]; nevertheless, the heart with supreme velocity strikes the lungs with its hardness. And so that it does not swell [too much], the lung has been given to the lungs <note>Leonardo likely means the lung tissue or the pulmonary system</note>; the branches of that vein proper to the heart are missing; rather, they unite with branches of the arterial vein of the spirit <note>original: "uena arteriale dell'anima"</note>, and the branches of the arterial vein strike against those of the vein of the heart, which strike causes the heart to refresh the spirit, maintaining it in life, as if the spirit were united with the life of the lungs, keeping the heart refreshed.

# On the path of the urine.
How the urine is separated from the blood by means of the kidneys, with the description of the vessels that go to these kidneys, and then through the passages <note>the ureters</note> that descend from the kidneys to the bladder.

<margin>
The portal vein, which originates from the spleen <note>original: "miza"</note> and liver and carries nourishment to the heart, originates below the liver from the branch of the vena cava; and it originates in the middle of the body in the front part with the cava and aorta, and passes under the stomach.
</margin>

<margin>
What the vena cava is, and what the aorta is.
</margin>

<note>Leonardo suggests a physical experiment using air and water to prove that the ureters are the one-way conduits for urine into the bladder.</note>

If you place a glass tube into the urinary opening of the bladder, and you place it from below under the water of a bucket, and you blow with your mouth into the tubes of the passages <note>the ureters</note> that come from the kidneys, many bubbles will come out of the bladder toward the surface of the water through the said glass. These bubbles are of air trapped by the mouth; and with the said blowing you will also see the bladder inflate and enclose within itself the said air. And by the said blowing you will also see the vessels of the kidneys originate through the middle of the section of that passage which sends the urine through the said passages to the bladder.

---

You shall do the same with the vena cava and the aorta: blow into one and the other, and you will see the vessels originate that go to the kidneys and those that go to the bladder. And from this you will clearly see how the urine is separated from the blood, and how the kidneys draw it to themselves and send it to the bladder.

<margin>
bladder
</margin>

He seeks to prove the mechanical separation of urine from blood through the vascular connections of the aorta and vena cava.</summary>

### FOLIO 13 — recto. [16.]

<margin>Man and related animals.</margin>
Man: the description of man, which includes those who are of a nearly similar species, such as the baboon, the monkey, and the like, of which there are many.

<margin>The lion and related animals.</margin>
The lion and its followers, such as panthers, lionesses <note>original: "leonze"; likely referring to a species of mountain lion or large feline</note>, tigers, leopards, (**cats**), lynxes <note>original: "lupi cervieri"; literally "deer-wolves," the historical term for the lynx</note>, Spanish cats, genets <note>original: "gannetti"; likely referring to the small spotted carnivore</note>, common cats, and the like.

The bull and its horned followers that lack teeth above, such as the buffalo, the deer, the fallow deer, the roe deer, sheep, goats, the ibex, musk deer <note>original: "mvcheri"</note>, chamois, and giraffes.

<margin>man</margin>
<margin>old age</margin>
Once the expansion of the lungs within themselves has occurred to refresh the air that enters them, it is necessary for the lung to grow in every 
<margin>youth</margin>
part; and having grown in every part, it is necessary that its circumference increases, from which it follows that the ribs

dilate, and once the ribs are dilated, they move away from one another; and such a moving away cannot happen without an increase 
<margin>anatomy</margin>

And this old man, a few hours before his death, told me that he had passed one hundred years, and that he felt no failure in his body other than weakness; and so, sitting upon a bed in the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence, without any other movement or sign of any mishap <note>Leonardo uses "accidente" to mean a sudden medical event or stroke</note>, he passed from this life. And I performed an anatomy <note>dissection</note> on him to see the cause of so sweet a death, which I found to come from a failing due to a 
<margin>veins of the old man</margin>
lack of blood and of the artery that goes to the heart and of the other supporting veins, which I found very arid, shriveled, and exhausted; which anatomy I described very diligently and with great ease, because he was deprived of fat and moisture <note>humors</note> which greatly impede the recognition of the parts. The other anatomy 
<margin>veins of the youth</margin>
was of a child of two years, in whom I found everything to be the contrary of that of the old man.

The veins in the old, through the thickening <note>original: "rinterramento," literally "earthing up" or silting up like a riverbed</note> of the vessels, grow thick and their membranes become so hard that they are deprived of all their movement, and the blood can no longer pass through them; from which it follows 
<margin>why the veins thicken</margin>
that such blood, with the percussion of the beating of the heart, wanting to pass through those veins—which, being made of hard skin, do not give way to such blood, nor do they dilate so that said blood can pass—wherefore by such an obstacle the blood is interrupted and turns back and strikes the walls of those veins and breaks them; and in such a way follows the death of that old man, and thus the course of life ends.

The veins in the young are like the skins of grapes, which have within them much moisture <note>original: "orina," likely a slip for "umore" (humor/moisture) or referring to the watery consistency of the fluid</note> and they dilate and contract by the movement of the blood that runs in them; but in the age of man those veins go on thickening, that is, putting on layers of skin, and losing their 
<margin>nutrition</margin>
movement, and they remain closed within themselves.
<unclear>The blood of the old does not have that liveliness and warmth that the blood of the young has, and this arises from its small quantity and its thickness.</unclear>

<summary>Leonardo describes his famous dissection of a centenarian at Santa Maria Nuova, concluding that death in old age is caused by the hardening and "silting up" of the veins (arteriosclerosis), which he contrasts with the flexible vessels of a two-year-old child.</summary>

...operation, one sees of them [the optic nerves] a weak effect during the day, and worse at night; and the aforesaid animals see better at night than by day—and the proof of this is seen because they hunt by night and sleep during the day, as nocturnal birds also do.

<margin>The pupil in nocturnal animals and in man.</margin>
The light, or pupil of the human eye, in its expansion <note>original: "cresscere"</note> and contraction, increases and decreases by half of its size; and in nocturnal animals it decreases and increases by more than a hundredfold its size. And this may be seen in the eye of the owl, a nocturnal bird, by bringing a lighted torch close to its eye, and even more if you make it look at the sun; for then you will see the pupil, which previously occupied the whole eye, diminish to the size of a grain of millet. And in such a state of diminution, it equals the pupil of man, and clear and bright things appear to it in the same color as they appear to man at that time; and all the more so, as the brain of such an animal is smaller than the brain of man; whence it happens that, as such a pu—

<column-break/>

...optics are thin and long and weak; and for that reason one sees them perform a weak operation during the day, and worse at night; and the aforesaid animals see better there at night than during the day; and the sign of it is visible, for they procure their prey at night and they sleep during the day, as nocturnal birds still do.

<margin>The pupil in nocturnal animals and in man.</margin>
The light, or pupil of the human eye, in its growth and in its diminution, grows and lacks half of its size; and in nocturnal animals it lacks and grows more than the hundredth part of its size; and one will see that in the eye of the owl, a nocturnal bird, by approaching a lit torch to its eye, and further, if you make it look into the sun, for then you will see its pupil, which previously held the whole eye, diminish to the size of a seed of millet, and in this diminution it equals the pupil of man, and clear and brilliant things seem to it of the same color as they appear during that time to man, and all the more so, as the brain of this animal is smaller than the—

<summary>Leonardo describes the extreme dilation and contraction of the pupils in nocturnal animals like owls compared to humans, noting how light intensity affects their vision and behavior. He concludes that an owl's pupil can shrink to the size of a millet seed when exposed to bright light, matching human proportions.</summary>

### ANATOMY — Folio B. 13 — Verso.

Just as in a piece of woven cloth, if the **warp** or the **weft** <note>Leonardo uses the textile terms "stame" and "trama" to create a mechanical analogy for biological tissue.</note> is broken in any part, that section becomes weak of itself and easy to tear. The same occurs in the composition of our flesh: where the warp or the weft of such flesh is lost, it becomes weakened. For this reason, nature has provided a multitude of branching nerves, veins, muscles, and other small cords, which intertwine through these branches in such a way that if one should weaken, another provides support.

Observe how the branches of the **vena chilia** <note>original: "vena chilia"; this is the Renaissance term for the vena cava, the large vein that returns blood to the heart.</note> open through the passages of the kidney's substance, and how the impurities of the blood are purged by means of the branches of the **emulgent vein** <note>original: "vena emulgente"; Leonardo refers here to the renal vein, which "filters" or "milks" (emulgent) the waste from the blood.</note>. See also how such impurities are sent to the bladder through the **ureter** passage.

---

<margin>
It is seen how the branch of the **vena chilia** is that which, by means of a transverse vein, joins with its opposite branch of the same vena chilia; and this transverse vein is that which sends branches to the kidneys, through which the kidneys are nourished.
</margin>

<note>The drawing on this page depicts the anatomical structure of the kidney, illustrating how the renal vessels (the branches of the vena cava) enter the organ. A modern archival number '68' is inscribed on the kidney itself.</note>

# Oh, how remarkable is the composition of the bladder, where there appears
to be neither beginning nor end to these urinary pores <note>original: "pori vrinari"; these are the ureters, the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder</note>, and how the urine does not return
from the bladder into the kidneys through the said urinary pores while the bladder,
with the help of other muscles, contracts to expel the urine from the bladder.
Since it does not return through the said urinary pores into the kidneys, the soul
<note>Leonardo often uses "the soul" or "nature" to refer to the guiding intelligence behind biological design</note>
provided that the urine could not be sent out of the bladder without
it exiting through the said urinary pores; therefore, she <note>the soul/nature</note> made it so that the said urinary
pores do not enter the bladder directly, but between one and the other
surface of the bladder, and they travel between the said membranes for some distance
through the thickness of the bladder.

As the urine attempts to return to the kidneys while the bladder contracts to send it
out through the member <note>the penis</note>, the urine within the bladder exerts pressure against the inner part
of the bladder and pushes and squeezes the two membranes of the bladder one against the other,
joining them together so that the entrance of the said pores
remains closed, and the urine cannot return inside except when the bladder
is not full of urine nor squeezed by other muscles.

# On the Function of the Bladder and the Passage of Urine

...s not return because as the bladder fills, the internal pressure of the liquid presses the membranes of the <term>tunic</term> <note>The inner lining or mucosal layer of the bladder</note> against the outer muscle, effectively sealing the ducts. Thus, the more the bladder is strained to expel its contents, the more firmly it closes the path back to the kidneys.

<column-break/>

->**The Mechanism of the Sphincter**<-

The exit of the bladder is governed by a powerful muscle which remains naturally constricted. It does not relax except when the will commands the expulsion of the waste, or when the volume of the urine overcomes the resistance of the fibers. Nature has designed this so that the weight of the fluid itself assists in the closure, ensuring that the body remains clean and the kidneys protected from the return of foul vapors.

<margin>
The muscle of the
bladder neck
acts as a gate,
opening only
when the soul
directs the
expulsive force
of the abdomen.
</margin>

### Observations on the Kidneys

The kidneys are situated against the spine, nestled within a bed of fat to preserve their heat. From each kidney descends a tube <note>the ureter</note> which carries the filtered water of the blood down to the aforementioned bladder. Note how the <insert>left kidney</insert> is often placed slightly higher than the right, a necessity dictated by the presence of the liver on the opposing side.

<table-header>
| Part of the Body | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| Kidneys | To filter the watery superfluity of the blood |
| Urinary Pores | To conduct the water to the reservoir |
| Bladder | To hold the water until it is convenient to expel it |
</table-header>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

...[if the urine] rose higher in the bladder than its entry—which is located near the middle of its height—it would follow that such an entry would immediately be closed. Consequently, no more urine could enter the bladder, and it would never fill beyond half of its capacity. Therefore, the rest of the bladder would be superfluous, and **nature does nothing in vain** <note>original: "la natura nõ fa nvl lla supfluita." This is a recurring axiom in Leonardo’s work, reflecting his belief that every anatomical structure has a necessary purpose.</note>. 

Therefore, we shall state—according to the 5th [proposition] of the 6th [book] on waters <note>Leonardo frequently applied his studies on hydraulic engineering and fluid dynamics to the movement of liquids within the human body.</note>—how the urine enters the bladder through a wide and winding path. Once the bladder is full, the <term>ureter pores</term> <note>original: "pori uritidi," referring to the openings where the ureters meet the bladder wall.</note> remain full of urine, and the urine inside the bladder cannot rise higher than its own surface while a man is standing upright. 

However, if he is lying down, the urine could return backward through these same pores; even more so if he were positioned upside down, which is rarely done. But lying down is very common; in that position, if the man stays on his side:

-> [Following the line drawn by Leonardo:] <-

one of the <term>ureter pores</term> remains on top and the other below. The one on top opens its entry and discharges the urine into the bladder, while the other pore below, due to the weight of the urine, is squeezed shut. Thus, a single pore is sufficient to provide urine to the bladder, provided that one of the <term>emulgent veins</term> <note>original: "vene mvlgntj," an archaic term for the renal veins. Leonardo uses "milking" (emulgent) to describe how the kidneys "draw" or filter fluid from the blood.</note> cleanses the blood of the <term>chyle</term> <note>original: "chilo," here referring to the watery byproduct of digestion that Leonardo believed was converted into urine.</note> of the urine.

---

...to spread and to return backward; a proof that is not true; for, if the urine rose in the bladder higher than its entry, which is near the middle of its height, it would follow that this entry would close immediately, and that urine could no longer enter the bladder, and that it would never exceed half of the capacity of that bladder; the rest of this bladder would therefore be superfluous, and nature makes nothing superfluous. 

We will say then, by the 5th of the 6th of the waters, how the urine enters the bladder by a wide and winding way, and when the bladder is full, the ureter pores remain full of urine, and the urine of the bladders cannot rise higher than its surface, the man remaining upright; but if he remains lying down, it could return backward through these pores, and more so if he put himself upside down, which is unusual; but being lying down is very usual, a position where, if the man remains on his side: 

-> [Following the line drawn by Leonardo:] <-

one of the ureter pores remains above, the other below; and... <note>This second section is a translation of the French transcription provided in the source, which mirrors Leonardo's Italian text above.</note>

### OF ANATOMY. — FOLIO B. — 14 VERSO.

### FOLIO 14 — *verso*. [173]

<margin>
Reason for the arrangement of the human intestine in relation to nutrition.
</margin>

Animals without legs have a straight gut, and this is because it always remains lying flat, since the animal does not rise up on its feet, as it does not have them; and even if it does rise, it immediately returns to a level position. But in man, this would not be appropriate because of his upright posture, for the stomach would empty itself immediately if the windings of the intestines did not delay the descent of the food. And if the bowels were straight, every part of the food would not be touched by the bowels, as happens in the winding bowels.

And thus much nutritive substance would remain in the superfluities <note>waste or excrement</note> of said food, which could not be sucked up by the substance of these bowels and transported into the mesenteric veins <note>original: "vene mjsseraice"; these are the veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</note>.

--- Page 211 ---
<meta>This page continues the anatomical investigation of the digestive tract. While the previous page focused on the physical pressure and mechanical expulsion of waste, this leaf provides a deep dive into the physiological "spirit" or vital force that drives the intestines. Leonardo here introduces a pioneering comparison between human peristalsis and the locomotion of an earthworm, moving from the macro-mechanics of the torso to the micro-mechanics of organ tissue.</meta>

Every organ of nutrition has within it a motion that arises from the <term>spirit<note>original: "spirito"; Leonardo refers to a vital force or nerve-like impulse believed to travel through the arteries to animate the organs.</note></term> which travels through the arteries. Thus, the motion of the intestine is through its entire length, by which the food descends. This is the true nature of the intestines. The urinary channels <note>the ureters</note> and every other natural organ through which any substance descends follow this same path. Even if this motion is not felt because of the <term>mesentery<note>original: "raneghamento dello schisimo"; likely referring to the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall, which Leonardo suggests masks the sensation of their movement.</note></term>, one can recognize in this discovery that the motion of the intestine is composed of two other motions: an internal motion and an external motion.

The internal motion is simply the narrowing of the tube, and the external motion is the shortening of it. Through this, just as mouthfuls are swallowed, the food is pushed forward throughout the entire path of the intestines. You can see this same thing happen to an **earthworm**: if you prick it with a needle through the middle of its bristle when it has stretched out, and push it toward its head, you will see the worm pull itself toward that push.

<margin>
The life of an organ’s nutrition is provided by the **artery**, because within it resides the "spirit" of that organ's movements. The **nutritive vein** <note>the portal vein</note> feeds the organ with refined food. This food is generated from the nourishment that enters the <term>ventricle<note>original: "uentricolo"; here meaning the stomach.</note></term> and travels almost through the whole length of the intestines via the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "vene miseraice"; the veins that transport nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note>. These veins then join the vein of the liver, which passes through the middle of said liver and through every part of it. And if coarse food remains in any part...
</margin>

<note>Annotation on the drawing of the esophagus:</note>
esophagus

<note>Annotation on the intestinal mass:</note>
intestines

<note>Annotation on the stomach:</note>
stomach

<margin>
The reason for this coiled arrangement of the **intestines** is so they may fit into a small space, and so the food does not travel too quickly to the exit. If it moved too fast, the belly would be able to extract very few of its nutritional virtues.
</margin>

...a membrane within itself. The **heart** is of this same nature, possessing motions from within and without, such that if one increases, the other decreases.

<summary>Leonardo describes the dual-motion (constriction and shortening) of peristalsis in the intestines, famously comparing it to the movement of an earthworm. He also explains how the mesenteric veins transport nutrients to the liver and provides a table of daily urine measurements.</summary>

### FOLIO 15 — *recto*. [18.]

<margin>Aponeuroses and muscular sheaths.</margin>
All the muscles of the body are wrapped in a very thin cartilage <note>original: *cartilagine*; Leonardo uses this term to describe what we now call fascia or aponeurosis</note>, and then they are converted into thicker cartilage and in that, they finish their extent.

<margin>Action of the transverse abdominal muscles on defecation.</margin>
The transverse muscles squeeze the intestines, but not the longitudinal ones, because if it were so, a man who is bent over and relaxes those muscles would not have the strength to perform the duty of pressing; but the transverse muscles never relax when a man bends, but rather they are pulled tight.

<margin>Muscles of the anterior abdominal wall and their function.</margin>
[Fig. 79:] n r b a S h m
*a b* are the last latitudinal muscles; and the membranes <note>original: *panniculi*</note> into which they are converted pass at a right angle under the longitudinal muscles *a m*.
