It is necessary to divide the motor <note>The "motor" here refers to the muscle groups responsible for movement</note> into several parts, and its maximum extension exceeds its minimum extension by a third part of one of its arms <note>original: "bracci" - a unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches</note>; and it does so even more as it creates a greater concavity of the arch in its back, as can be seen with these acrobats <note>original: "giocolatori"</note> who bend so far backward that they join their hands together with their feet. <margin>Pectoral muscles.</margin>
*b* terminates at the beginning of the <term>humerus</term> <note>original: "osso dell'aiutorio"; literally "the bone of aid," a medieval term for the upper arm bone</note>, and it serves as a support for the ribs and the <term>thorax</term> <note>original: "toragie"</note> of the chest.

<margin>Rules for the demonstration of the muscles of the chest.</margin>
The demonstration of the rib cage requires first the simple ribs, bare, with the spaces between them open; then the muscles that connect to their sides, by which they are linked together; then the muscles woven over them, which serve the movements of expansion and contraction of those ribs; in addition to this, the other muscles placed transversely over the aforementioned muscles, which serve various movements from different perspectives.

[Fig. 87 :] *n b*.

<margin>Reason for the movement of the ribs.</margin>
On the extreme raising and lowering of the shoulders, which assists the movement of the ribs. Because the extreme raising and lowering of the shoulders, by means of the muscles of the neck fixed to the <term>vertebrae</term> <note>original: "spondili"</note> of its spine, prevents—when those shoulders are raised—the movement of the ribs in their descent; and when such shoulders <unclear>descend</unclear>... <note>The text here breaks off, likely continuing the mechanical explanation of how shoulder position limits or enables the expansion of the lungs.</note>

<summary>Leonardo outlines a systematic method for dissecting the chest, suggesting a layer-by-layer approach from the bare ribs to the complex overlapping muscles. He also notes the mechanical relationship between shoulder movement and the expansion of the rib cage during breathing.</summary>

# STUDIES ON LIGHT AND SHADOW

In sunlight, the shadow of the same object will be shorter the closer it is to the sun’s zenith <note>original: "polo del sole"; Leonardo uses the 'pole' to refer to the central point of the light source or the point directly overhead</note>. Furthermore, the shadow of an object of lesser height will be shorter than that of an object of greater height.

<margin>
This happens because of the angle: one is obtuse, the other is acute.
</margin>

<note>Study of light falling on a curved surface labeled a, d, c.</note>

<margin>
The air that heats the shadow will be less cooled by the air cooled within the shadow than the shadow itself. This cooled air is descending and cools the shadow in such a way that, between the cooled air and the cooled shadow, there will be no difference at all between the air and the shadow.
</margin>

The function of the shadow’s cone <note>the conical volume of space cast into shadow by an object</note> is to cool the air in that region. Because the air is cooled, it gains more weight, and for this reason, it descends. Through this descent, it displaces the air within the shadow; this air, being moved and cooled, strikes the earth with its motion and cools the surrounding air.

---

<note>Geometric study of shadow lengths (onbra) relative to angles from the sun's position (polo del sole).</note>

Because the ratio of **d f** is closer to the perpendicular of the line **d c** than is the line **e d** in **d c f d**. By **d f**, it is found to be near a half-circle, and the line **d e** will be between two angles, one acute and the other obtuse. Therefore, the line **d e** is longer than the line **d f**. And **e** will be closer to the sun's zenith **d d** than is the line **d f**. Therefore, the shadow of **d e** will be shorter than the shadow of **d f**.

<margin>
The shadow of the same object will be shorter the closer it is to the sun's zenith. Furthermore, the shadow will be shorter for an object of lesser height than for an object of greater height, assuming they are at equal distances from the sun's zenith.
</margin>

<term>shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra"; Leonardo studies shadows not just as an absence of light, but as a physical volume of air with its own properties.</note>
<term>sun's zenith</term> <note>original: "polo del sole"; the highest point or the source of the light rays.</note>
<term>cooled air</term> <note>original: "aria rinfrescata"; Leonardo observed that shadows are not just visual, but thermal phenomena, causing air to become denser and sink.</term>

<summary>On this page, Leonardo demonstrates through geometry that the length of a shadow depends on the height of the object and its proximity to the sun's zenith. He also posits a proto-scientific theory of thermodynamics, suggesting that the "cone" of a shadow cools the air, making it heavier and causing it to descend and circulate.</summary>

<keywords>optics, shadows, geometry, thermodynamics, atmospheric movement, sun's zenith, light and shade</keywords>

<margin>The Lung.</margin>
<margin>Inspiration.</margin>
(It is asked) when the lung has sent out the air <note>original: *vento*, literally "wind"</note> and its volume decreases by as much as the air that was exhaled from it, one must then investigate from where the space in the chest cavity—created by the shrinking lung—draws air to fill that gap, seeing as in nature a vacuum <term>vacuo|The Aristotelian concept that "nature abhors a vacuum," meaning a space cannot be truly empty</term> does not occur.

<margin>Expiration.</margin>
And it is further asked: from where, during the expansion of the lung, does it drive the air out of its receptacle? By what path does this air escape, and once it has fled, where is it received?

<margin>Mechanism of breathing. Action of the intercostal muscles.</margin>
The lung remains always filled with a certain quantity of air, even though it has expelled the air required for its exhalation; and when it refreshes itself with new air, it presses against the ribs of the chest, dilating them somewhat and pushing them outward. This can be seen and felt by placing one’s hand upon the chest during breathing, as the chest expands and contracts.

<summary>Leonardo investigates the mechanical process of breathing, questioning how air moves to fill the space in the chest cavity according to the principle that nature does not allow a vacuum.</summary>

--- Page 247 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s anatomical investigation into the respiratory system. While the previous page focused on the mechanical lubrication of the heart via the pericardium, this page shifts to the thermodynamics of breathing—specifically how the lungs draw in external cool air to regulate the heat generated by the heart.</meta>

The air that occupies the lung always remains outside of it when the lung contracts, and it enters again when the lung expands, because air occupies empty spaces; and from every place where it departs, it rushes back in with instantaneous speed. From this, it necessarily follows that the air with which the lung fills itself is not the same air that has just exited.

It is necessary that the air entering the lung be from that which stays outside the <term>mouth</term> <note>original: "bocha"</note> and not from that which has just exited, because if it were from the air that exited, it could not be—

<note>Anatomical study of the human lungs and trachea</note>

<margin>
The lung contracts and by that means pushes the air out; and when the chest expands, the lung expands due to its multitude of vessels of the <term>pulmonary vein</term> <note>original: "arteria venosa"; in Leonardo's time, the pulmonary vein was often called the "venous artery" because it carries oxygenated blood to the heart, unlike other veins</note>. These vessels are like a sponge that fills with air, and <term>thus</term> <note>original: "chosi"</note> they cause the lung to swell and expand. The lung, being filled with air, causes the bones of the chest to expand.
</margin>

<margin>
To this, reason responds that the lung grows thick to refresh the chest and to push the breath out.
</margin>

Because if it were from the air that exited, that air would be heated by the heat of the chest, and that heat would not serve to cool the blood that is heated in the lung by the <term>impetus</term> <note>original: "impito"; referring to the forceful, energetic motion or "fury" of the heart's action</note> of the heart. This impetus is what heats the blood with great fury, and to cool it, cold air enters from outside. Therefore, if the air that entered were that which had just exited, it would enter warm and would not cool it at all. From this it follows that when we blow on a candle, there is much of this lukewarm air, and it is not that which cools the blood for the reason stated above. It is necessary that, in order to push out the air that is inside, the lung contracts and becomes smaller through the force of the chest bones.

---

Thus, one must conclude that the air entering is that which stays outside the face—that is to say, from the lower lip—and not that which has exited, because that is hot and exits with an impetus that drives it far away, and none of it can be taken back in unless we were to put our face into the chest of another.

On the movement of air inside and outside the <term>mouth</term>.

<summary>Leonardo argues that the primary purpose of breathing is to draw in cool external air to regulate the heat generated by the heart's "fury," noting that the lungs must expand like a sponge to facilitate this cooling process.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, respiration, lungs, heart, blood cooling, pulmonary vein, thermodynamics, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

### ON ANATOMY — SHEETS B — 18 RECTO.

->FOLIO 18 — recto. [28 21.]<-

<margin>
Precepts for anatomical demonstrations.
</margin>

Remember to never change the boundaries <note>original: "termini"</note> of any limb because of any muscle that you might remove in order to uncover another. Even if you remove muscles whose attachments <note>Leonardo uses the word "termini" to refer to both the ends of the muscles and the structural outlines of the body part.</note> form the boundary of a part of the limb from which you detach them, you must then mark with frequent dots the boundary of that limb which was removed by the separation of any muscle. You shall do this so that the figure of that limb which you are describing does not remain a monstrous thing <note>Meaning a distorted or unrecognizable shape.</note> for having had its parts taken away. Furthermore, from this follows a greater knowledge of the whole; for once the part is removed, you see in the whole the true shape of the place from which it was taken.

->FOLIO 18 — recto. [28 21.]<-

<margin>
Origin and course of the nerves of the lower limb from the sacral plexus <note>The sacral plexus is the network of nerves that provides motor and sensory components to the posterior thigh and most of the lower leg and foot.</note>.

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

<note>This page features Leonardo da Vinci's anatomical studies of the human leg and foot. It focuses on the calf muscles (the gastrocnemius and soleus) and the Achilles tendon, analyzing their mechanical function in lifting the heel. Leonardo uses both a naturalistic rendering and a schematic lever diagram to explain the biomechanics of movement. The letters $m, n, r, s, t, f, l, o, p, q$ in the text correspond to specific anatomical features and mechanical points indicated on the drawings.</note>

<margin>
$m\ n\ r\ s\ t\ f\ l$

Muscle $n\ r$, by whose function the heel is raised, shall be of great power <note>original: "potenzia"</note> since it is so long and so thick and goes into $n\ m$.

$p\ r\ s\ q\ t$

these are <term>tendons</term> <note>original: "corde" — Leonardo often used the word for "cords" or "strings" to describe tendons and ligaments</note> and muscles that raise the foot.
</margin>

<margin>
$m\ l\ o\ p\ q\ r\ s\ n$

It does not swell <note>original: "rinfia" — a Renaissance variant of "gonfia," referring to the contraction of a muscle belly</note> for any reason, therefore it is not a muscle; you will see this [to be true] against those who say the muscle underneath has the function of raising the heel.

Muscle $m$ swells in $n$ and pulls upwards, and muscle $r$ does the same.

And $q\ n\ o\ p$ are muscles that serve to keep the <term>sole of the foot</term> <note>original: "pianta del piè"</note> level, so that one does not pull more than the other.

If muscle $p$ should swell, it must not pull more than $q$, because if $n$ pulled more than $o$, the sole of the foot would face inward <note>original: "drento"</note>.
</margin>

<note>Leonardo's observation that certain structures do not "swell" (contract) led him to distinguish between the fleshy, active belly of a muscle and the passive, fibrous nature of a tendon. His diagrams here treat the foot as a lever, where the calf muscles provide the force necessary to lift the weight of the entire body through the heel.</note>

<summary>This page explores the biomechanics of the human calf, specifically how the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles work together to lift the heel and maintain a level foot. Leonardo applies mechanical principles to anatomy, viewing the tendons as cords and the foot as a lever system.</summary>

<keywords>anatomy, biomechanics, calf muscles, Achilles tendon, gastrocnemius, sole of the foot, muscular contraction, Renaissance science</keywords>

**Study 100**
This illustration provides an anatomical study of a human leg, viewed from a side-posterior angle. Leonardo’s drafting highlights the surface definition of the thigh muscles, the functional articulation of the knee, and the natural curvature of the calf. This study is characteristic of his analytical approach, where he sought to document how muscles shift and tension changes through various poses.

**Study 99**
This more focused sketch details the posterior (back) view of the thigh and knee region. Leonardo emphasizes the popliteal area—the "pit" or hollow behind the knee—and the arrangement of the surrounding muscle groups. This reflects his method of isolating specific joints and muscle clusters to better understand the structural mechanics of the human machine.

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

### Page 126

<margin>Precepts for the demonstration of the bones and muscles of the leg.</margin>
...if they were cut, and which are of lesser importance; and you shall do this for each limb.

Note the proportionality of the bones between one another —

and the purpose for which each serves —

In this demonstration, made from various perspectives, account is taken of all the muscles that move the leg; these muscles are attached to the edges of the <term>pelvis</term> <note>original: "alchatĩ" or "catino" (basin) — anatomical terms derived from Arabic or colloquial Italian used by Leonardo to describe the pelvic basin</note>, where the muscles that move the thigh from the knee upward also originate.

And also <insert>of those</insert> that bend the leg when kneeling.

->Noting<-

<margin>Notes regarding the muscles that are revealed and hidden during movement.</margin>
Different muscles reveal themselves in the different movements of animals, and different muscles are those which, in such a diversity of motions, are hidden; and on this subject, it is necessary to write a long treatise for the purpose of identifying the locations injured by wounds, and also for the use of <term>sculptors</term> <note>original: "statuari"</note> and painters, etc.

<summary>Leonardo outlines instructions for illustrating the leg's musculoskeletal system, emphasizing the importance of pelvic attachments and the changing appearance of muscles during movement. He notes that these anatomical studies are essential for medical diagnosis of wounds and for artists to depict the body accurately.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, leg muscles, pelvis, kinesiopathology, artistic anatomy, Leonardo da Vinci, proportions</keywords>

# ON ANATOMY — FOLIO B — 20 RECTO

->noting<-

<margin>Origin of the movements of the leg and the feet.</margin>
All the movements of the leg <note>Leonardo uses "gamba" (leg) here to refer specifically to the lower leg/shin area</note> arise from the muscles of the thigh; which movements are the cause of bending such a leg, and straightening it when bent, and turning it to the right and to the left.

But the movements of the feet are caused by the muscles originating in the leg; of the movements of the toes, part arise in the leg and part in the feet.

<margin>Insertion of the motor muscles of the leg.</margin>
And <insert>of</insert> of the motor muscles of the leg, part arise in the hip and part in the thigh; and the true location of all of them shall be given.

->Noting.<-

<margin>Origin of the movements of the leg and the feet.</margin>
All the movements of the leg arise from the muscles of the thigh, which movements are the cause of bending the leg, and of straightening and turning the bent leg to the right and to the left.

But the movements of the foot are caused by the muscles originating in the leg; as for the movements of the toes, a part of them arises in the leg and a part in the foot.

<margin>Insertion of the motor muscles of the leg.</margin>
And as for the motor muscles of the leg, a part of them arises at the hip, and a part in the thigh; and the true location of all will be given.

<summary>Leonardo describes the mechanical relationship between muscle groups and limb movement, noting that thigh muscles move the leg, while leg muscles move the feet and toes. He establishes his intent to map the precise anatomical "location" or insertion points of these muscles.</summary>

And these cords <note>referring to tendons</note> move without the movement of the muscles because nature sends the nerves to the brain, and the muscles remain for the viscera, just as the feet of birds and jumping animals have their strength in the muscles of the thighs.

<note>Anatomical study of the leg muscles, showing the thigh and knee joints from multiple perspectives.</note>

<margin>
All muscles originate from the bone, and their tendons attach to the other bone; and there are some that originate from the nerve and end in the nerve, and some that emerge from it.
</margin>

<margin>
The nerves and the muscles have no passage in the places where they pass in the locations where the bone is, because the nerves and muscles would attach themselves to the bones, and this will be demonstrated.
</margin>

->It is not, however, that the muscles<-
->do not pass over the nerves,<-
->but the nerves pass through the middle.<-

<margin>
Do not bind the nerves because they go to the brain, but bind the muscles because they are the ones that pull the cords <note>tendons</note> of the <term>manfura</term> <note>likely a transcription error for 'manovra' (maneuver/operation) or 'misura' (measure)</note> of the muscles; and when the movements have their power by means of the muscles because they end in <unclear>cords</unclear>.
</margin>

The muscle of the inner thigh, which fills the void made by the two thighs, is of the same nature as the muscle of the arm called the <term>lacerto</term> <note>A Renaissance term for a specific bundle of muscle fibers, often referring to the biceps or similar powerful muscles</note>; wherefore such a muscle, wishing to leave its site and thicken, reduces the narrowness of the void, at times retracting and causing the muscle below to thicken.

But the thigh bone does not remain bare in the places where there are no muscles, since in such places pass the nerves and the veins that carry nourishment to the muscles, bones, and skin exceeding the nature of the bones; because if it were otherwise, it would be necessary for the nerves to pass through the bones, whereby they would not be suited for movement.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the mechanical relationship between muscles, tendons, and nerves in the thigh, comparing human anatomy to that of birds and explaining how nerves must remain free from bone attachments to facilitate movement.</summary>

# ON ANATOMY — FOLIO B — 20 VERSO

<margin>
Demonstration of the instrumental figure of man. <note>Leonardo views the body as a "machine" or "instrument" governed by mechanical laws.</note>
</margin>

We shall demonstrate this instrumental figure of man in [blank] figures, of which the first 3 will be the ramification <note>The branching structure or arrangement</note> of the bones; that is, one from the front, which demonstrates the width of the positions and shapes of the bones; the second will be seen in profile, and will show the depth of the whole and of the parts and their position; the 3rd figure will be a demonstrator of the bones from the back. Afterward, we shall make 3 other figures in similar views, with the bones sawn through, in which one will see their thickness and hollowness. We shall make 3 other figures of the whole bones and of the nerves <note>In this period, "nerves" often referred to both nerves and tendons</note> that arise from the nape of the neck, and into which members they branch. And 3 others of the bones and veins, and where they branch; then 3 with muscles, and 3 with skin and proportioned figures; and 3 of the female, to demonstrate the womb and menstrual veins that go to the breasts. <note>Leonardo followed the ancient belief that a direct vascular connection existed between the uterus and the breasts to transform menstrual blood into milk.</note>

<margin>
Demonstration of the instrumental figure of man.
</margin>

We shall demonstrate this instrumental figure of man in figures, of which the first 3 will be the ramification of the bones, that is: one from the front, which demonstrates the width of the positions and shapes of the bones; the second will be seen in profile, and will show the depth of the whole and of the parts and their position; the 3rd figure will be a demonstrator of the bones from the back. Afterward, we shall make 3 other figures in similar views, with the bones sawn through, in which one will see their thickness and hollowness; 3 other figures we shall make of the whole bones, and of the nerves, which arise from the nape of the neck, and into which members they branch; and 3 others of bones and veins, and where they branch; then 3 with muscles, and 3 with skin and proportioned figures, and 3 for the female, to demonstrate the womb and menstrual veins, which go to the breasts.

->Order of the Books<-

<note>Leonardo often titled sections of his notebooks as "Order of the Books" to indicate how he intended to organize his various scientific treatises on subjects like water, light, or anatomy.</note>

<note>First block of text discussing the interaction of wind and water waves</note>
If the water is moved by the wind, and furthermore the motion of the air causes movement in the waves of that water, I say that if the air moved by the wind is joined with the air moved by the waves of the water, it will be much faster at the points of contact than one motion of the air would be without the other; and this is proved by the 10th <note>original: "per la .10. di questo"</note> proposition of this treatise.

<note>Short note on wave velocity</note>
Because the wave will be that much faster as it is narrower; and if by chance the wave of the water is moved by the wind—

<note>Detailed section citing the 11th proposition of his treatise</note>
Because if, according to the 11th [proposition] of this, the air is moved by the wind and also the air is moved by the wave of the water, I say the air will be faster at the points of contact with that wave of water; and it will be that much faster as the wave is narrower at its <term>knee<gloss>original: "ginochio" — Leonardo's term for the crest or the curve of the wave peak</gloss></term>; and it will be that much narrower as it is higher; and it will be that much higher as the wind is more powerful.

And if it is higher and also narrower, the air will be even faster at the contact points of the knee of that wave.

---

<note>Bottom block of text refining the previous observations</note>
<margin>
~
~
~
~
~
~
~
~
<note>These marks in the margin may serve as placeholders or indicate a vertical scale for the diagrams.</note>
</margin>
I say further that if the wave of the water is moved by the wind, and the wave of that water is struck by the wind, I say the air will be faster at the knee of that wave than in any other part of that wave; and this will be according to the 11th [proposition] of this. Because the wave will be that much higher as the wind is more powerful; and the air will be that much narrower <note>Leonardo is describing the "Venturi effect" or aerodynamic compression: as the air is forced over the peak of the wave, the space it occupies is constricted, causing it to speed up.</note> as the wave is higher; and it will be that much faster as the air is narrower; and furthermore, the air will be that much faster as the air of that wave is more moved and joined with the air of the wind.

<note>Vocabulary list from the original manuscript: water, wind, wave, air, knee (crest), movement, contacts, eleventh, order of the books.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of waves, proposing that wind velocity increases at the wave's crest (the "knee") due to the compression of air as it passes over the rising water. He references specific propositions from his own developing treatise on fluid dynamics to explain how wind power and wave height are interconnected.</summary>

The higher the step that a man climbs, the further forward his head will be relative to his upper foot.

To weigh more at *a* than at *b*, this man will not be on step *m*; the line *a f g* demonstrates this.

[Fig. 112 :] *f a b g m* <note>This refers to a diagram showing the center of gravity during a climb.</note>

<margin>Posture when stopping a run.</margin>
[Fig. 113.]

When a man wishes to stop his run and exhaust his momentum <term>impeto: the physical force or energy of a moving body</term>, necessity makes him lean backward and take small, quick steps.

<margin>Mechanism of certain movements of the human body, and foundations of human statics.</margin>
The center of weight of a man who lifts one of his feet from the ground always remains above the center of the sole of the foot that stays planted.

<margin>Mechanism of climbing.</margin>
A man climbing stairs shifts so much of his weight forward and to the side of the higher foot that he provides a counterweight to the lower leg; thus, the effort of that lower leg is limited only to moving itself.

The first thing a man does when climbing steps is to unload the weight from the leg—

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the biomechanics of climbing and stopping, noting how the body shifts its center of gravity to maintain balance and overcome momentum. He explains that climbing requires leaning forward to counterbalance the weight of the trailing leg.</summary>

...the leg that he wishes to lift, [unloading it] of the weight of the torso that was resting upon that leg; and, in addition to this, he loads the opposite leg with all the rest of the man's mass, together with the other leg. With that momentum <term>impeto: the force or energy of a moving body</term>, he raises himself up, and at the same time extends the arm <note>original: "ℬ.", an abbreviation for *braccio* (arm)</note> which he was resting upon the knee; this extension of the arm pushes the torso and the head upward, and thus straightens the curved back.

# ANATOMY — Sheets B.

### 21 — Verso.

A man’s foot cannot be lifted unless the weight above is first positioned over the axis <note>original: "canna", literally 'cane' or 'shaft', referring to the vertical line of the leg</note> of the other leg, in such a way that the **center of gravity** falls over that leg. This is because if the weight were distributed equally between both feet, he would be unable to lift either one of them without first shifting his weight onto the sole of one or the other.

A man who wishes to climb a **step** <note>original: "scaglione"</note>:
If the step is equal to the length of the thigh <term>femur</term> from the hip to the knee, it would be impossible for a man to climb it unless he assists himself by bending his back, using his arms, and employing the helpful movement of his head; furthermore, he must throw his torso forward over the leg that is placed upon the step.

<margin>
<note>Figures 110 and 111: These sketches show a human figure from the front, illustrating how the body must lean to one side to shift the weight onto a single leg before the other can be raised.</note>
</margin>

He who wishes to climb a step, before he actually ascends, bends his back and throws his torso forward along with his arms, so that his **center of gravity** is positioned over the foot that is stepping up.

<margin>
<note>Figures 112 and 113: Profile drawings showing the deep forward lean of the torso and the positioning of the limbs required to maintain balance while ascending a high vertical height.</note>

<margin>
->On Motion<-
A man never moves by his own will if he does not first shift his center of gravity. <note>Leonardo uses "center of gravity" (centro della sua gravezza) to describe the point where the body's weight is balanced; movement, for him, is a controlled loss of balance.</note>
</margin>

<note>The following text is translated from Leonardo's mirror script, converted to standard reading order.</note>

Let a man who is some distance away from the spot from which he must jump be of the same nature as a stone thrown from a sling; in the first stages of its motion, the stone goes on charging itself with power <note>original: "potenzia" — here referring to kinetic energy or momentum</note>, which it then discharges at the point where it strikes. So does the man who runs in order to jump: if he had to jump from one level plane to another level plane, he would go on charging himself with power during that run, and then he would discharge it at the moment of the jump, lifting with that jump his entire weight along with that power acquired in the run.

That part of the man will be of lesser weight which is furthest from his center of gravity.

 the man who jumps will be as much lighter in weight as the force of the muscles employed in such a jump is great—which force is greater than the weight of the entire man.

<margin>
On jumping or motion
On jumping upward
</margin>

<note>Studies of human kinetics, focusing on the center of gravity during jumping and stepping.</note>

A man who jumps upward from a level plane sinks down as much in preparing the motion as he raises himself at the end of his jump.

Whatever part of the man moves during the jump, that part which is moved is what gives motion to the whole body; such as the arms, which in jumping are raised with speed, and the head likewise.

A man who climbs up a ladder or another difficult place cannot lift himself unless he first leans his torso forward, so that his center of gravity is positioned over the foot that supports the body.

And if a man wished to climb without leaning his torso, it would be necessary for his center of gravity to be above the tip of his foot, which is impossible for a man to remain in equilibrium.

### On the Rule of the Step

When a man climbs a ladder or a steep hill, he must first shift his center of gravity forward, beyond the foot that is planted, so that the weight of his body assists the muscles of the leg in lifting the rest of the frame. If he does not do this, the effort will be twice as great, for the muscles must then both lift the weight and maintain the balance.

<margin>
On the center of gravity
</margin>

The man who carries a heavy burden on his shoulders must lean his body in the opposite direction of the weight, so that the combined center of gravity of the man and the burden falls directly over the soles of his feet. <note>original: "centro della gravezza" — Leonardo’s recurring term for the balance point of a system.</note>

<column-break/>

### On the Force of the Jump

A man who jumps from a stationary position cannot jump as far as one who takes a running start. This is because the man who runs acquires a certain amount of accidental force <note>original: "forza accidentale" — a term used in pre-Newtonian physics to describe momentum or kinetic energy imparted to an object</note> which, when added to the natural force of his muscles, allows him to overcome the resistance of his own weight with greater ease.

<margin>
->The Physics of the Leap<-
</margin>

Observe the dancer: when he wishes to leap high into the air, he first crouches low, compressing his body like a spring. The lower he sinks, the higher he may rise, for the extension of the legs must be equal to the contraction that preceded it. <note>This reflects Leonardo's observation of the "action and reaction" principle in biological movement.</note>

<gloss>The weight is always moved by a force greater than itself.</gloss>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

...in the spleen, as with that branching <note>referring to the way blood vessels divide and spread</note>; since in the young the veins are straight and full of blood, and in the elderly they are twisted, flattened, wrinkled, and empty of blood.

<margin>Senile alterations of the liver.</margin>
And so it is with the liver, which in youth is usually colorful and of uniform consistency; and in the elderly it is pale, without any redness of blood. The veins remain empty, and within the matter of this liver—<note>Leonardo originally wrote *polmone* (lung), then corrected himself to *fegato* (liver)</note>—this matter can be compared, in its thinness, to bran soaked with <insert>a little</insert> water, and thus it easily disintegrates. By washing it, one leaves the veins that branch within it clear and free of any substance of the liver.

<margin>Stomach and peritoneum.</margin>

<margin>Senile alterations of the liver.</margin>
... in the spleen, as with this branching; the veins being straight and full of blood in the young, while in the old they are twisted, and faded, and wrinkled, and void of blood.

And likewise the liver, which in youth is usually colored and of a consistent toughness, and in the old is pale, without any redness of blood, and the veins remain empty; and within the matter of this <term>liver parenchyma<note>original: "pedicone"; Leonardo uses this term to refer to the functional tissue or "flesh" of the organ as opposed to the vessels.</note></term>, which matter can be compared to orange-colored bran soaked with a little water, and thus it easily falls apart when washed, leaving the veins that branch within it cleared [...] of every substance of the liver.

<margin>Senile alterations of the liver.</margin>
<note>This is a French translation of the Italian text above, likely added by a later 19th-century editor of the manuscript.</note>
in the spleen, as this branching, the veins being straight and full of blood in young people, and in the elderly they are twisted, and crushed, and rough, and empty of blood.

And so the liver, which in youth is usually colored and of an equal tenacity, and in the elderly it is pale, without any redness of blood, and the veins remain empty, and among the matter of this (parenchyma) liver, which matter can be compared, by its thinness, to bran, soaked in a little water, and so it willingly breaks up, by washing it, and it leaves the veins, which branch inside it, cleared [...] of all substance of the liver.

### FOLIO 23 — recto. [31 44]

<margin>The cervical spinal cord, the nerves that originate from it, and the spinal membranes.</margin>
[Fig. 119 :] The spinal cord <note>original: *nuca*. In Leonardo's time, this term referred to the spinal cord or the medulla, rather than just the nape of the neck.</note> and the nerve born from it.

These two membranes <note>original: *scorze*, literally "barks" or "shells"</note> that clothe the spinal cord are the same ones that clothe the brain—namely, the <term>pia mater<gloss>the delicate, innermost membrane</gloss></term> and the <term>dura mater<gloss>the tough, protective outer membrane</gloss></term>.

<margin>The origin of the cervical nerves.</margin>
[Fig. 120 :] 2nd thorax. <note>likely referring to the second section of his study on the torso</note>
Vertebrae <note>original: *spondili*, a Latinate term for the bones of the spine</note> of the neck, sawn and removed from the center forward, revealing the site of the spinal cord and how it resides and branches out from these vertebrae.

<margin>Anatomical and functional relationships between nerves and muscles.</margin>
The substance of the spinal cord enters, for some distance, into the origins of the nerves, and then follows the hollow <note>original: *forato*. Leonardo shared the contemporary belief that nerves were tiny tubes or pipes through which "animal spirits" or sensations flowed.</note> nerve to its final ramifications. Through this hollow channel, sensation is carried into each muscle. Every muscle is composed of as many other minute muscles as there are fibers into which that muscle can be divided; and each of these smallest muscles is wrapped in membranes <note>original: *paniculi*</note> that are almost imperceptible, into which the final branches of the aforementioned nerves are converted. These [nerves] obey— <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Leonardo investigates the structure of the cervical spinal cord and its protective membranes (the meninges), proposing a mechanical theory where nerves act as hollow tubes that transmit sensation to the individual fibers of a muscle.</summary>

FOLIO 24 — recto. [32]

### Order of Anatomy

<margin>
Rules for the topographical demonstration of the upper limb, and especially of the hand.
</margin>

First make the bones, that is to say the arms, and place the motor <note>Leonardo uses "motor" to refer to the muscles or tendons that initiate movement.</note> from the shoulder to the elbow along all the lines; then from the elbow to the arm; then from the arm to the hand, and from the hand to the fingers.

And in the arm, you shall place the motors of the fingers that open; and these, in their demonstration, you shall place alone. In the second demonstration, you shall clothe these muscles with the second motors of the fingers; and you shall do this step by step, so as not to cause confusion. But first, place upon the bones those muscles which are joined to those bones, without any other confusion of other muscles; and with those, you shall place the nerves and veins that nourish them, having first made the tree of the veins and nerves upon the simple bones.

# ANATOMY — Sheets B.

If the "tooth" <note>original: "dente"; Leonardo uses this term to refer to the fleshy belly or the specific attachment point of a muscle</note> of the muscles were that which moved the bones where those muscles are attached, nature would not have created the nerves, nor the <term>sarti</term> <note>literally "tailors"; here Leonardo refers to the tendons or cord-like attachments</note>, but the "tooth" of the muscles alone would have been sufficient to move the bones. But I say that the nerve is that which pulls the "tooth" of the muscle along with the muscle, and the muscle pulls the bone by means of the cord or rather the <term>sarto</term>; therefore, the nerve is that which pulls, and the muscle is that which thickens and shortens itself, drawing to itself the cord into which it is converted, and pulls the bone where that cord is attached. And if it were the case that the nerve pulled the muscle and the muscle pulled the bone, you would see the muscle become thinner, because both ends of the muscle would move away from each other; but the contrary is seen, that is, that the muscle thickens and shortens.

<margin>
125
<note>Small diagram consisting of an acute angle with an arrow pointing to the vertex, which is labeled with the letter 'A'.</note>
</margin>

### Of the nerves of the fingers of the hand.
The cords <note>tendons</note> that move the fingers of the hand are 24, which pass under the ligament of the bone of the hand, called the <term>bracciale</term> <note>the transverse carpal ligament or "bracelet" of the wrist</note>. Of these 24 cords, 12 move the fingers outward, and 12 move them inward; and these cords are moved by 24 muscles placed in the shafts of the <term>sesta</term> <note>the radius and ulna</note> of the arm.

### Of the nerves.
The nerves that move said muscles are 4. Two of which move the muscles that move the fingers outward, and the other 2 move the muscles that move the fingers inward. And note that the nerves are not cords, but are the <term>sentimenti</term> <note>sensory perceptions or impulses</note> and powers of movement and of <insert>speech</insert> <note>original: "dicitura"; likely referring to the command or "telling" the limb to move</note>; and the cords are the others, which have neither feeling nor power, if they were not pulled by the muscles, and the muscles would not move if they were not pulled by the nerves. Therefore, the nerve is that which gives movement and feeling to the muscles, and the muscle pulls the cord, and the cord pulls the bone.

<summary>Leonardo explains the mechanical chain of movement where nerves trigger muscles to contract (thicken), which in turn pull tendons to move the bones of the hand. He identifies 24 tendons in the wrist controlled by muscles in the forearm, distinguishing between the "feeling" nerve and the "mechanical" tendon.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, kinesiology, tendons, nerves, muscles, hand anatomy, biomechanics, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

# On the Motion of the Crossbow
<note>original: "del moto d’ebreo" - likely a transcription error for "del moto d'ebro" or "del moto d'arco" (of the motion of the bow). Given the context, it refers to the mechanical action of the weapon.</note>

The power of the bow will always be of the radius of the circle of which the string **a.b.** of the crossbow is the chord. And let **c.** be the nut <note>The 'nut' is the rotating component that holds the bowstring until the trigger is pulled.</note> of the stock, and **d.** and **f.** be the bow, and **g.** and **h.** the two ends of the bow fixed in the stock **i.** I mean to say that the power of such a bow will always be related to the radius of the circle of which that bow is a part; and because the ends of the bow describe a circle of which the bow is a part, which has for its center the string that keeps it bent, and this will always be the case in the motion of shots made through the air.

---

The motion will always be in the same manner through the air.

<note>Schematic diagram of a crossbow illustrating the mechanical forces and levers involved in its tension.</note>

If you wish to see how much force is in that string which is pulled to release the bow, you must know that the crossbow requires a thick string so that it is less elastic. You must see what proportion the distance from the middle of the pulled string to the stock has to the distance from the middle of the string to the end of the bow; and that will be the proportion of the power of the bow to the power of the string. I mean to say that if from the middle of the bow to the nut is 1 braccio <note>A 'braccio' (arm) is a Renaissance unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm.</note> and from the end of the bow to the middle of the string being pulled is 1 inch, then that proportion will be the force of the string to the force of the bow. Thus, if the bow has a force of 100 pounds, the string has a force of 12 pounds. Or rather, if you want to pull 100 pounds of force on a string of a bow that holds 1200, the proportion must be as 1 inch is to 12 braccia. And this is where it is weakest; for if the string is closer to the stock, it will be weaker, and if it is further away, it will be stronger, because the bow will be less bent. Therefore, you see that at the end of the string's travel the bow is fully bent, and at the beginning it is not bent at all. For this reason, the bow is made thinner at the ends than in the middle, because the ends must make a greater movement than the middle and must be lighter.

<term>Crossbow (balestra)</term>, <term>string (corda)</term>, <term>bow (arco)</term>, <term>nut (noce)</term>, <term>stock (manico)</term>, <term>force (forza)</term>, <term>radius (raggio)</term>, <term>circle (circolo)</term>, <term>pounds (libre)</term>, <term>braccia (braccia)</term>, <term>inch (oncia)</term>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the mechanical physics of a crossbow, calculating the ratio of force between the bow and the string based on geometric proportions. He explains that the bow's ends must be thinner and lighter to accommodate their greater range of motion during a shot.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, ballistics, crossbow, leverage, geometry, physics of motion, Renaissance engineering</keywords>

# On the Motion of the Crossbow

The power of the bow will always be of the radius of the circle of which the string **a.b.** of the crossbow is the chord. And let **c.** be the nut <note>The 'nut' is the rotating component that holds the bowstring until the trigger is pulled.</note> of the stock, and **d.** and **f.** be the bow, and **g.** and **h.** the two ends of the bow fixed in the stock **i.** I mean to say that the power of such a bow will always be related to the radius of the circle of which that bow is a part; and because the ends of the bow describe a circle of which the bow is a part, which has for its center the string that keeps it bent, and this will always be the case in the motion of shots made through the air.

---

The motion will always be in the same manner through the air.

<note>Schematic diagram of a crossbow illustrating the mechanical forces and levers involved in its tension.</note>

If you wish to see how much force is in that string which is pulled to release the bow, you must know that the crossbow requires a thick string so that it is less elastic. You must see what proportion the distance from the middle of the pulled string to the stock has to the distance from the middle of the string to the end of the bow; and that will be the proportion of the power of the bow to the power of the string. I mean to say that if from the middle of the bow to the nut is 1 braccio <note>A 'braccio' (arm) is a Renaissance unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm.</note> and from the end of the bow to the middle of the string is 2 braccia, the power of the string will be double the power of the bow.

<margin>The weight of the bolt <note>A 'bolt' or 'quarrel' is the short, heavy arrow used in a crossbow.</note> must be proportional to the strength of the wood.</margin>

Furthermore, one must consider the weight of the bow itself, for if the bow is too heavy, its own mass consumes the speed of its recovery, and the bolt will not be cast with the desired velocity. <insert>The swiftest motion is that which finds the least resistance from the instrument itself.</insert> Therefore, the master of the engines <note>term: 'master of the engines' (maestro d'ingegni) - a military engineer or designer of war machines.</note> must balance the thickness of the wood with the tension of the cord to achieve the perfect strike.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the mechanical advantage of the crossbow, calculating how the geometry of the drawn string and the length of the bow arms determine the force exerted on the projectile.</summary>

->FOLIO 25 — recto.<-

<margin>Reaction of the pupil to the stimulus of light: dilation and contraction.</margin>
The pupil of nocturnal animals varies from a large to a greater size, according to the great or greater darkness of the night.

<margin>The pupil in nocturnal animals.</margin>
The pupil of these same nocturnal animals also varies from small to smaller, according to the great or greater brightness of the day.

From what has been said, it is concluded that these nocturnal animals always possess an equal power of <term>visual faculty</term><note>original: "virtù visiva." In Leonardo’s time, this referred to the "power" or "spirit" of sight that was believed to reside in the eye.</note> throughout all the variations of brightness or darkness that may occur during the day or night.

<margin>The pupil in relation to the visual faculty.</margin>
The visual faculty is present in the whole pupil and in every one of its parts.
It follows that half of the pupil sees an object as completely as if the pupil were whole.

The larger the size of the pupil, the larger the form and the greater the clarity with which it will see its object; and conversely, the smaller it is, the smaller and darker it will see that object.

The pupil of nocturnal animals varies from a large quantity to a larger one, according to the great or greater darkness of the night.

<margin>The pupil in nocturnal animals.</margin>

It follows that by closing an eye, the visual power is diminished for it by half, and this test is made in luminous bodies, like the sun, the moon, the stars, and also in a light or fire.

This diminution of clarity will be seen without closing one of the eyes; but instead of closing it, let one interpose the hand or the finger before one of the pupils, between the air and the eye, and you will see a quantity of air with the 2 pupils, which will meet with the air seen by a single pupil, and the air which is seen by one pupil will be all the more obscure than that which is seen by 2 pupils. ->Let a rod of wood be made which is fixed in the middle of a shaft, which rod should be <unclear>by</unclear> half of its thickness, and let it be fixed to this shaft by its center, and let the shaft be fixed upon 2 supports, and let the said rod and the shaft be made to move together with the same motion.<-

And if this rod were turned by its edge, it would go with its thinness against the air and would have great force; and if it were turned crosswise, it would go with its thickness against the air and would lose much of its force; and if it were turned by its face, it would go with its face against the air and would lose much more force.

# ON ANATOMY — SHEET B — 26 RECTO

->FOLIO 26 — recto<-

The foot is a masterpiece of engineering and a work of art. <note>Leonardo often marveled at the mechanical efficiency of biological structures.</note> Observe how the weight of the man is distributed upon the ground through the **calcaneus** <term>heel bone</term> and the heads of the **metatarsals** <term>the long bones leading to the toes</term>.

### On the Motion of the Toes

The tendons that descend from the leg serve to elevate the foot and to move the toes with great strength. <margin>Note the tension of the cords during the leap.</margin> When the heel is raised from the earth, the weight of the entire body rests upon the ball of the foot. 

<column-break/>

The bone of the leg, which is called the **tibia** <term>shinbone</term>, rests its weight upon the **astragalus** <term>talus or ankle bone</term>. This bone acts as a pivot for the entire machine of the foot. 

*Of the muscles of the calf:*
These muscles are the primary movers when a man stands upon his toes. <insert>They are thicker in those who carry heavy burdens.</insert>

| :--- | :--- |
| **Calcaneus** | Support of the heel |
| **Astragalus** | Hinge of the ankle |
| **Phalanges** | Balance and propulsion |

<margin>Precepts for the topographical demonstration of the muscles of the back.</margin>
You shall make a rule and measurement for each muscle, and you shall give an account of all their functions <note>original: "uffizi"</note>, and in what manner they are used, and what moves them, etc.

[Fig. 129.]

# ON ANATOMY — SHEETS B — 27 VERSO

->FOLIO 27 — verso.<-

<margin>On the method of representing the neck.</margin>
The highest parts of lean bodies are the highest in the muscular, and similarly in the fat; but the difference in the shape of the muscles that the fat have compared to the muscular will be described here below. 

And where the muscles are separated from one another, you shall show the boundaries of their beginnings and their ends; and if you should find any muscle that appears to be one but is actually two, as occurs with the <term>trapezius: the large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck</term>, you shall represent it as such.

[Fig. 130.]

[Fig. 131.]

<insert>Note the cords of the neck.</insert>
You shall first draw the bones of the neck, which are seven, and similarly those of the chest; then you shall draw the muscles that move the head, and those that move the neck, and those that move the shoulders and the arms. 

<margin>On the nerves and veins.</margin>
After you have drawn the muscles, you shall draw the nerves that give sensation and movement to these muscles, and the veins and arteries that nourish them. You shall show how these nerves arise from the <term>nucha: the spinal cord</term> <note>original: "nucha," a medieval term derived from Arabic used to describe the spinal marrow</note> and how they penetrate the muscles.

<column-break/>

->FOLIO 27 — verso.<-

<margin>On the movement of the head.</margin>
Observe how many muscles move the head, and how many move the neck, and how many move the shoulders. You will find that the muscles which move the head are different from those which move the neck, although they are often joined together. 

[Fig. 132.]

[Fig. 133.]

<gloss>The muscle that raises the shoulder.</gloss>
The muscle that raises the shoulder is the same one that lowers the head when the shoulder is fixed; and if the head is fixed, it raises the shoulder. Thus, you must describe the <term>antagonism: the way muscles work in opposing pairs</term> of these movements.

<unclear>The depth of the pit of the neck</unclear> varies according to the movement of the arms and the tension of the muscles called the <term>sternocleidomastoids: the prominent muscles on the sides of the neck</term>.

<margin>Intercostal muscles, external and internal, and their function.</margin>
The <term>mesopleuri</term> <note>From the Greek 'mesos' (middle) and 'pleura' (side/rib); these are the small muscles located between the ribs.</note> are the small muscles placed between the ribs, dedicated to the expansion and contraction of those ribs; and these two contrary movements are designed for the drawing in and breathing out of air in the lungs, which are enclosed within the ribcage. The expansion of these ribs arises from the external muscles of the ribs, which are positioned along the slant *m n*, with the help of three muscles *o p q* which, by pulling the ribs upward with great power, enlarge their capacity, in the same way that <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

capacity in the same way that is seen in the ventricles <note>The lower chambers of the heart</note> of the heart. But the ribs, having to return downward, could not descend by themselves while a man is lying down, were it not for the internal muscles <note>The internal intercostal muscles located between the ribs</note>, which have an obliquity <note>An angled or slanted direction</note> contrary to the external muscles; this obliquity extends along the line *f n*.

->On the power of the intercostals<-

The office <note>The function or purpose</note> of the external intercostals <term>mesopleuri: a Renaissance anatomical term for the intercostal muscles located between the ribs</term> is to raise and dilate the ribs, and they are of marvelous power in their situation; seeing as they are established, with their upper extremities, upon the spine itself where the jointed ribs originate, and their obliquity descends toward the navel.

Let this bone of the neck be made first with its spinal medulla <note>original: *nucha*, a term Leonardo used here to refer to the spinal cord or the vertebral canal</note> as is shown here above, and then without the spinal medulla, to give a true understanding of the whole neck, which will consist of 4 parts.
And for each part, let 3 views <note>original: *ditioni*, meaning perspectives or aspects</note> be shown—that is, from below, from above, and from the sides—and then let them be shown joined together in their proper alignment with the bone that supports them. And the same should be done for the bones of the chest <term>petto: the thoracic cage or sternum and ribs</term> and likewise for the whole spine <term>spina: the vertebral column</term> of the back and for each of its joints. Then let them be put back together, reconnecting them with their nerves <note>Leonardo often used *nervi* to mean both nerves and tendons</note> and with their ligaments, and then let them be clothed in their muscles. And so, stage by stage, one will see the figure grow until reaching a complete understanding of the whole; and this will be done in 4 demonstrations for each part of the whole man.

The spirit of these senses <note>The "vital spirits" or impulses believed to travel through the nervous system</note> descends from the bone of the neck through the external nerves, and not through the same holes from which the spinal marrow <note>the spinal cord</note> emerges, as happens with the senses of the arms, and as happened with the senses of sight, hearing, smell, and taste, which emerged through holes in the skull <note>original: *nucha*, used here to refer to the base of the skull or the posterior cranial fossa</note>.

<summary>Leonardo outlines a rigorous, four-step method for anatomical illustration—from individual bones to the fully muscled body—and notes the distinct pathways of the nerves as they exit the spinal column and skull.</summary>

### On the power of the intercostals.

The function of the external intercostals is to raise and dilate the ribs, and they have an admirable power in their position; since they are fixed, with their upper extremities, to the same spine where the articulated ribs originate, and their slant descends toward the navel.

...is seen to occur in the ventricles of the heart; but the ribs, having to return downwards, could not descend by themselves, the man remaining lying down, if it were not for the intrinsic muscles which have the contrary orientation to the extrinsic muscles, which orientation extends along the line f a.

### On the power of the intercostals.

The office of the external intercostals is to lift and dilate the ribs, and they have an admirable power in their situation; for they are established, with their last upper extremities, upon the spine itself, where the slender ribs <note>The French translator used *côtes déliées* for the Italian *disnodate*, suggesting "un-knotted" or "slender"</note> are born, and their orientation descends toward the navel.

-> On the position of the muscles <-

<note>Leonardo's anatomical studies of the human ribcage, focusing on the mechanics of respiration and the arrangement of intercostal muscles. The text is written in his characteristic mirror script.</note>

<margin>
These are the first muscles that open the ribs for breathing, and there are 8 of them.
</margin>

<margin>
Which pull the rib below to the one above.
</margin>

The muscles of the ribs are divided into two parts, namely into upper muscles and lower muscles. The upper ones are those that pull the ribs upward, and the lower ones are those that pull them downward. And these are further of two kinds: those that are placed on the outside of the rib and those that are placed on the inside of the rib. Those placed on the outside are called external intercostal muscles <term>intercostali esterni: muscles located between the ribs that aid in inhalation by lifting the ribcage</term>, and those on the inside are called internal intercostal muscles <term>intercostali interni: muscles that assist in forced exhalation by depressing the ribcage</term>. These have different functions because one of them serves to expand the ribs and the other to contract them—that is, for breathing and for the expulsion of air from the lungs. And these muscles are always crossed with one another, so that those on the outside are shaped like the letter "n" and those on the inside like the letter "m," or rather like an "X." <note>Leonardo is describing the "obliquity" or diagonal slant of the muscle fibers; the fibers of the internal and external intercostals run in opposite directions, creating a cross-hatched pattern that provides structural strength.</note>

-> On the proportion of movement <-

The movement of the rib is greater at its end than at its beginning. This is proven by the logic of the triangle, because the longer side moves more than the shorter one; that is, the further a point is from its center of motion <note>original: *centro di moto*, referring here to the pivot point or joint where the rib meets the spine</note>, the more it moves. Thus, the rib moves more at its end <note>The "end" refers to the front of the rib cage near the sternum, while the "beginning" refers to the vertebral attachment.</note> than at its beginning.

<note>The sketches below show the thorax from different angles, illustrating how the ribs act as levers. Leonardo treats the human body as a machine, applying the laws of physics and geometry to biological functions.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the mechanical function of the intercostal muscles in respiration, explaining how their opposing diagonal orientations allow for the expansion and contraction of the chest. He applies geometric principles to show that the front of the ribcage moves more extensively than the back during breathing.</summary>

### FOLIO 28 — recto. [8]

<margin>Reason for the relationship between the fingers of the hands and the toes of the feet.</margin>
[Fig. 133.]

Every prominence formed by the joints of the toes and the fingers has a corresponding concavity in the adjacent digits which receives that protrusion within itself. Nature has created this so as not to distort their width; for if these protrusions were in direct contact with one another, the feet would become of a great width. Furthermore, one of two effects would be necessary: either that the digits were all of the same length, or that one had two joints and the other only one, as will be demonstrated in the proper place concerning the bones.

It follows here:

[Fig. 134.]

[Fig. 135.]

<margin>Duration of the movement of a liquid.</margin>
The motion of a liquid, made in any direction whatsoever, proceeds in its initiated revolution for as long as the <term>impetus</term> <note>original: "linpeto"; the force or momentum transferred to an object</note> given to it by its first mover remains alive within it.

<summary>Leonardo explains how the joints of fingers and toes are designed to nestle into adjacent cavities to maintain a narrow shape, and notes that liquid motion continues only as long as its initial momentum persists.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, joints, fingers, toes, skeletal structure, fluid dynamics, impetus, momentum</keywords>

<margin>
The body of the animal continually dies and is reborn.

Nourishment in relation to life.
</margin>

The body of anything that nourishes itself continually dies and continually is reborn, because nourishment cannot enter except into those places where the past nourishment has expired <note>original: "esspirato"; used here to mean used up or departed, like a breath leaving the body</note>. And if it has expired, it no longer has life; and if you do not restore nourishment equal to the nourishment that has departed, then life fails in its vigor; and if you take away that nourishment, life is completely destroyed. But if you restore as much as is destroyed day by day, then as much of life is reborn as is consumed; similar to the light made by the candle with the nourishment given to it by the moisture <note>original: "omore"; referring to the melted wax or tallow acting as a liquid fuel</note> of said candle. This light also, continually, with a very rapid defense, restores from below as much as is consumed above in dying, and in dying it is converted from a splendid light into dark smoke. This death is continuous, just as the smoke is continuous; and the continuity of such smoke is equal to the continuous nourishment, and in an instant the whole

## STUDIES OF THE FOOT AND ANKLE

...arises doubled above the inner joint <note>the medial malleolus or inner ankle bone</note> of the foot, as is seen in the drawing below of the left leg. This nerve <note>original: "neruo"; in Leonardo's time, the term was used interchangeably for nerves, tendons, and ligaments, as they all appeared to be cord-like structures that transmitted force or sensation.</note> originates from the outer joint of the knee, passes through the interior to the inner joint of the foot, and becomes doubled, turning into 4 nerves. The reason for it passing through the interior is to provide movement to the 4 inner toes. And the nerve marked **"s"** becomes a single one that goes above the big toe <note>original: "pollice del piè"; literally "the thumb of the foot."</note>.

<note>Dorsal view of a human foot showing the tendons extending to the toes.</note>

These nerves on the upper surface are those that lift the tip of the foot upward; and within these nerves there are others that perform the same function.

<note>Small anatomical study of the heel bone (calcaneus) and a schematic diagram of the arch of the foot.</note>

### ON THE MOVEMENT OF THE TOES
#### LATERAL MOVEMENT

The lateral movement <note>side-to-side motion</note> of the feet arises from nerves which originate from the outer part of the leg bone <note>the fibula</note> at both heads of the knee. One of these passes beneath the inner bone of the ankle <note>the medial malleolus</note>, and the other passes outside the other ankle bone <note>the lateral malleolus</note>. The one that passes inside is what pulls the toes inward diagonally toward the other foot, and the one that passes outside is what pulls the other toes outward toward the outer ankle.

Of these, more shall be written in the <term>Treatise on Nerves</term> <note>Leonardo's proposed but never completed masterwork on human anatomy</note> and on the muscular masses, veins of every limb, and every one of their movements; and to what use every minimum part of bone or nerve is put, and the service performed by each of the muscles of the joint of the feet, and likewise of the toes.

The upward movement of the 4 smaller toes arises from the muscles which are placed above the shin bone <note>the tibia</note> on the outer side of the said shin. These muscles send their nerves <note>tendons</note> under the ligament <note>the extensor retinaculum, or "the band of the foot"</note>, which pass over the bridge of the foot and divide into 4 heads which come to attach to each of the 4 toes on the upper side. 

However, those toes that move downward <note>flexion</note> originate from the muscles of the calf of the leg. They pass under the inner ankle of the foot and go under the sole of the foot, dividing into 4 heads and attaching to each toe on the underside. The big toe also moves by itself, performing its movement upward, downward, and laterally on its own.

<margin>Muscles of the tongue.</margin>
### On the muscles that move the tongue

No member <note>Leonardo uses "member" to refer to any distinct part or organ of the body.</note> has need of such a great number of muscles as the tongue; of which there are 24 known, besides the others that I have discovered. And of all the members that move by voluntary motion, this one exceeds all others in the number of its movements *(and sensations)*.

<margin>Comparison with the other sensory organs.</margin>
And if you wished to say that the office of the eye is to receive all the species <note>original: "spetie"; in Renaissance science, this refers to the "images" or "forms" emitted by objects that travel to the eye.</note> of the infinite shapes and colors of the objects placed before it, and the sense of smell in the infinite mixture of odors, and the ear of sounds; we shall say that the tongue also senses infinite flavors, simple and compound. But this is not to our purpose, as we make it our profession to treat only of the local motion of each member.

<margin>Here he will treat only the movements of the tongue.</margin>
<margin>Mechanism of speech. Variety of languages. Tendency toward the infinite.</margin>
Consider well how, by means of the motion of the tongue, with the help of the lips and teeth, the pronunciation of all the names of things <insert>is created</insert>.

### On the nerves of the lungs, the heart, and other internal organs.

If a man who moves his arm or foot or any other limb is doing so with great effort, and if he must sustain that effort for a long time, it is necessary that his breath be suspended. This is because if the breath were <unclear>not</unclear> suspended, he would be unable to expel the superfluous smoke <note>Leonardo uses "smoke" or "fumes" to describe the metabolic byproducts of the heart's heat</note> that is generated by the heat of the heart, and thus the heart would be suffocated. However, if the man who moves the limb does so lightly, without effort or fatigue, then it is not necessary for his breath to be suspended.

</margin>

Now, if the soul is in the heart, it must be in the muscles of the heart, because the heart is a muscle; and if it is in the muscles of the heart, that same soul will also move the muscles of other parts, which are composed of the same substance...

# On the turns of birds

Of the offices <note>technical term: "uffitii" — here meaning the specific mechanical functions or duties</note> that the various members of the bird perform in the act of its flying, there are three kinds: of which the first is to go forward; the second is to lower or raise itself; the third is to turn. Therefore, regarding these three, we shall speak separately of the reason. Of the birds that circle through the air at a height by the force of the wind without beating their wings, many are seen; and among these, there is no difference of motion except by the lowering or raising of one of the wings, or indeed the wings and the tail together. In these motions, the matter is of great difficulty to explain, because it is composed of infinite and tiny winds <note>Leonardo refers to "venti" here as localized air currents or turbulence</note>, of which some are stronger and some less, and they are of infinite variety of positions and motions. Of these we shall speak at the end of the primary members of the birds, which, in mounting <note>original: "mōtādo" (montando) — climbing or ascending</note> without beating their wings, rise so high that it seems they remain still in the air. In which it is to be noted that if the bird has no wind, it cannot do this. Therefore, with the tip of the wing turned to the wind, and the other wing doing the same, it rises in a screw-like motion <note>original: "a uite" — literally "like a screw" or spiral</note>; but if it did not do so, it could not do it unless it had the wind. And when the wind strikes the wing from below, it does not rise unless it gives it a certain slant <note>original: "pieghatura" — a fold or inclination</note>, whereby the wind strikes the underside of the wing at an angle <note>original: "per l'obiecho" — obliquely</note>, and by this way the bird rises and mounts on high. When the wind comes to it from behind, the wind always strikes it on the underside and in the rear, because when it rises, the wing is slanted in a certain way, and by this way it rises. And at other times it rises by virtue of the front toward the wind, giving a certain slant to the wing by which the wind pushes it upward; but this is when the bird wishes to lower itself or to go forward. But when it wishes to mount, it always turns its breast to the wind, and the wind always strikes it from below. And this is when the bird, always beating its wings, goes always mounting; and beating the wings, the wind comes to it straight on. But without beating the wings, it is necessary that the wind comes at an angle, and this is of much variety; whereby the wind always strikes it from the underside and from the rear. And this mounting it does when the wind comes to it straight on, giving it a certain slant, whereby the wind strikes it in the underside and in the rear. And this mounting, by turning the wing with the tip to the wind, it does without beating the wings, turning itself around and always mounting. And when the bird lowers itself, it does so without beating the wings, flying toward the wind; and this is when the wind strikes it on the top and in the front. And when it lowers itself beating the wings, the wind always strikes it on the top and in the front, and by this way it lowers itself whenever it wishes. And when the wind strikes it straight on, it lowers itself beating the wings, by which way it always lowers itself. And whenever it rises by beating the wings, it is by virtue of the wind, which wind strikes it straight on, giving a certain slant to the wing, by which it always rises. Thus it always rises and lowers itself in infinite varieties, of which mounting and lowering the bird always does by the virtue of the wind and by the virtue of the wings and of the tail; therefore of all these we shall speak separately.

# ON ANATOMY. — SHEETS B. — 29 RECTO. 179

### FOLIO 29 — recto. [*5 41*]

<margin>
Muscles of the lips, the reason for their abundance.
</margin>

->Of the muscles that move the lips of the mouth<-

The muscles that move the lips of the mouth are more numerous in man than in any other animal; and this arrangement is necessary for him because of the many operations in which these lips continually exercise themselves, such as in the 4 letters of the alphabet *b f m p* <note>These are labial consonants, which require specific lip movements to pronounce</note>, as in whistling, in laughing, in weeping and similar actions; then in the strange distortions which buffoons <note>original: "buffoni" — entertainers or mimics</note> use in mimicking faces.

</margin>

->ends are brought close together?<-

<margin>
Muscles of the lips, the reason for their abundance.

FOLIO 29 — recto. [*5 41*]

Of the muscles that move the lips of the mouth.

The muscles that move the lips of the mouth are more numerous in man than in any other animal; and this arrangement is necessary in him for the many operations in which these lips continually exercise themselves, such as in the 4 letters of the alphabet *b f m p*, as in whistling, in laughing, in weeping and similar actions; then in the strange distortions used by buffoons in mimicking faces.

<margin>
Muscles of the mouth and their function; mention is made of the orbicularis of the mouth, the depressor of the lower lip, the elevator of the upper corner, the risorius, and the buccinator.
</margin>

Which muscle is it that squeezes the mouth so that its lateral ends are brought close together.

[Fig. 136 :] *a b*.

The muscles that squeeze the mouth, decreasing its length, are in the lips themselves; rather, these lips are the very muscles that close themselves. It is true that the muscle constitutes the lip.

The muscles that move the lips of the mouth are more numerous in man than in any other animal; and this arrangement is necessary for him because of the many operations in which these lips continually exercise themselves, such as in the four letters of the alphabet *b f m p* <note>These are labial consonants, which require specific lip movements to pronounce</note>, as in whistling, in laughing, in weeping and similar actions; then in the strange distortions which buffoons <note>original: "buffoni" — entertainers or mimics</note> use in mimicking faces.

<margin>
Muscles of the mouth and their function: mention of the orbicularis oris <term>orbicularis oris: the circular muscle surrounding the mouth</term>, the depressor of the lower lip, the elevator of the upper corner, the risorius <term>risorius: the muscle used for smiling</term>, and the buccinator <term>buccinator: the cheek muscle used for blowing</term>.
</margin>

->Which muscle is it that squeezes<-
->the mouth in such a way that its lateral<-
->ends are brought close together?<-

---

[Fig. 136 :] a b
The muscles that squeeze the mouth by decreasing its length are in the lips themselves; or rather, these lips are the actual muscles that close themselves. It is true that the muscle composes <note>original: "dechonpone" — likely meaning "constitutes" or "makes up the structure of"</note> the lip.

# ANATOMY — SHEETS B.
## 29 — Recto

<margin>
136
<note>Figure 136: A schematic diagram illustrating the anatomy of the glottis and larynx, likely included by a later editor to accompany the text.</note>
