<note>The following sections contain Leonardo da Vinci’s anatomical observations, originally written in his characteristic mirror script. He examines the mechanical properties of air within the respiratory and circulatory systems.</note>

->**Whether it is possible for the air to pass from the lung to the heart or not.**<-

No, because air by itself can neither condense nor rarefy except through heat or cold, or by percussion <note>original: "perchussione" — a forceful striking or impact</note> or the force of a motor <note>Leonardo uses "motore" (motor/mover) to refer to the biological mechanisms, such as muscles, that initiate movement</note>. If air were condensable by the force of a motor, it would then follow that as the lung becomes small and constricts its vessels <term>vasi: the bronchial tubes and blood vessels of the lungs</term>, the air contained within them would become condensed; and that small part of spirit <note>original: "spirito" — referring to the 'vital spirit,' which Renaissance thinkers believed was a refined substance produced from air in the heart</note> which is found in the heart would also be condensed by the constriction of the heart and rarefied by its dilation. And if it were rarefiable and condensable, it would make the heart muffled <note>original: "sordo" — literally 'deaf,' meaning the sound of the heart striking the chest wall would be dampened or silenced by the air</note> as it strikes the wall of that ventricle, and it would delay its opening, because that ventricle could not open unless that air were first rarefied; and if it were not rarefied, it would resist the dilation of that ventricle.

->**On expiration and how the air leaves the lung.**<-

Air leaves the lung through the constriction which the lung itself performs, which by the force of muscles attached to its walls pulls inward and constricts its vessels, whereby the air is forced to leave. And this same thing happens to the heart in its constriction.

That part of the heart which is situated between one ventricle and the other <note>the interventricular septum</note> provides within itself the strength of the wall for said ventricles in their constriction; but if it were perforated <note>original: "bucata" — Leonardo is questioning the common belief of his time that the heart's septum had tiny pores allowing blood or air to pass between sides</note>, as some believe, so that air from the lung might pass into the left ventricle to cool the blood, <unclear>and as said air cannot [pass] without condensation, nor the ventricle without dilation</unclear>... <unclear>for if such air were condensable, it would become condensed during the constriction of that ventricle</unclear>...

<note>Leonardo’s vocabulary for this study includes: **polmone** (lung), **core** (heart), **aria** (air), **ventriculo** (ventricle), **chondensare** (to condense), **rarefare** (to rarefy), **dispirazione** (expiration/breathing out), **muscholi** (muscles), and **vasi** (vessels).</note>

<summary>Leonardo argues against the idea that air passes directly from the lungs into the heart, using mechanical reasoning about the compressibility (condensation and rarefaction) of air. He describes the muscular action of the lungs during expiration and questions the existence of pores in the heart's septum.</summary>

<keywords>anatomy, heart, lungs, respiration, ventricles, compression of air, vital spirit, cardiac septum</keywords>

The nature of the air enters the lungs, and being very cold, it refreshes the body; and the moisture of the lungs moistens the air, making it heavier and of a different nature than the external air that enters. But the air is cooled by the nerves between the ribs, and in the lungs, a sixth part of the air that enters through the opening of the lungs is retained. This is what nourishes the <term>vital spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance physiology, the "vital spirit" was a refined substance thought to be produced in the heart and distributed via the arteries to provide life and movement.</note>, which, between the lungs and the mouth, changes its nature through the help of the heat of the heart; it becomes thinner and lighter, and of a different "species" than the external air. This air then returns to the lungs as vapor and smoke through the mouth. And just as the moisture of the air fills with the appearances <note>original: "spetie"</note> of things, however small, even the smallest, so the appearance of this air nourishes the vital spirit. That which "smokes" is that sixth part which was said to be retained in the lungs; from it, the nerves of the lung are nourished, and they move by the power of that sixth part of the air retained in the lungs. This air then exhales through the pores of the outer layer <note>original: "scorza"</note>. Those nerves of the lung are what move the lungs to refresh themselves; they are not what move the ribs, because the ribs are moved by the nerves that originate from the <term>nucha</term> <note>The spinal cord or the nape of the neck.</term>. These are the ones that pull the nerves that open the lungs to draw in air, and those that pull the ribs to open the space where the lung can expand. This shall be proven in the book of <term>anatomy</term>. And just as the moisture of the air that enters the lungs is purged through the mouth, so the part of the air that has been purged of its smallest appearances through the nerves of the lungs is purged through the pores of the outer layer of the lungs.

### 30 — Recto.

<note>The following text is transcribed from Leonardo's mirror writing, presented here in normal left-to-right reading orientation. It concerns the synchronous movement of respiratory muscles.</note>

->On the principle of the movement of the diaphragm<-

All the muscles move at one and the same time and cease at one and the same time; for if they were separate, they would go on changing the position of the ribs of the <term>spine</term><note>original: "schina"; Leonardo uses this to refer to the vertebral column and the back</note> in one part at a time, which would be contrary to the intention of the movement of the spine.

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

The voice <note>original: "Lauocie"</note> and movement would be given by the friction of a dense body in a dense body, or a dense body rubbed against the air <note>original: "confreghata... nellaria"</note>, which is the same thing. This friction of the dense with the rare <term>rare: a substance of low density, like air, as opposed to "dense" solids</term> condenses the rare and makes it resistant. Furthermore, when the fast-moving rare and the slow-moving rare condense against one another at their points of contact, they produce a sound or a very great noise. The sound or murmur made by the rare moving within the rare with moderate movement is like the great flame that generates sound within the air. The very great noise made by the rare with the rare occurs when the fast-moving rare penetrates the immobile rare, like the flame of the fire exiting a cannon <term>bombarda: an early type of cannon or mortar</term> and striking the air; and also the flame exiting a cloud which strikes the air in the generation of lightning bolts <note>original: "saette"</note>.

<margin>Not possible for the spirit without the movement of air.</margin>
Therefore, we shall say that the spirit cannot generate a voice without the movement of air, and there is no air within it, nor can it expel air from itself if it does not have it. And if it wishes to move that air in which it is infused, it is necessary that the spirit multiply, and it cannot multiply if it has no quantity <note>Leonardo argues that a spirit, being incorporeal, lacks "quantity" (volume/mass) and therefore cannot displace or compress air to create sound.</note>. # ON ANATOMY — FOLIO B — 30 VERSO

...says that no rare <term>rare: a substance of low density, such as air or gas</term> substance moves itself unless it has a stable place from which to take its leverage. This is especially true when an element must move within its own element <note>For example, air moving through air, or water through water</note>, which does not move on its own except by uniform evaporation at the center of the evaporated thing. This is similar to what happens with a sponge squeezed in the hand held under water; the water escapes in every direction with equal movement through the gaps between the fingers of the hand that squeezes it.

<meta>While the previous page (200) focused on the anatomical structures of the heart, this page (201) shifts abruptly to Leonardo’s studies of optics and atmosphere. ## You will proceed with knowledge so that by three additions of knowledge, no one
## is certain of the other, because you will go so far through the eye that they see.

### Rule of Seeing
### Concerning the shadow of every body

The air between the eye and the object seen varies in 3 ways. The first is as the eye moves away from the shadow, which will be much darker the closer it is to the eye, and will be much lighter the farther it is from said eye. The reason is this: if the air is uniform in itself, its darkness will be greater as it has greater thickness <term>grosseza</term> <note>original: "grosseza," meaning the volume or mass of atmosphere between the observer and the object.</note>. Therefore, the shadow is darker when it is closer; that which is farther is lighter because there is less air <note>Leonardo argues that the "darkness" of air itself competes with the shadow of an object; the more air between you and a shadow, the more the shadow's distinctness is lost.</note> between the eye. And if said air is uniform in itself, no other variation will exist except the moving away.

The shadow will be less dark as the air is clearer; as the eye moves away from the shadowed part, so much less light will be seen as it is closer to the air. The air will be less dark the closer it is to the shadow, and it will be darker the farther it is from that shadow. The reason is that air is in itself of equal inherent darkness, and where it exists in lesser thickness, it will be less dark, and it will be darker where it exists in greater thickness. 

A shadow will be darker when it is within a lesser thickness of air—that is, when it is closer to the eye—and it will be less dark when it is farther from that eye. See how the distant length of the air will be less dark, and as said air is closer, it will be lighter; and less shadow will be seen through the air between the eye and the shadow, because there will be so much air less darkened that it will be seen. That shadow will be seen through the lesser thickness of air, which will be so much less dark because of the lesser thickness of air. The other will be lighter as it is farther from said eye, and so much less dark because it is less obscured by the air; because it is less obscured by the air, it will be so much lighter as it is seen through a lesser thickness of air, and so much darker as it is seen through a greater thickness of air. 

And as the air is clearer, the shadow will be less seen; the air of a cloth or other body <note>Leonardo is considering how different materials interact with the atmospheric "veil."</note> will be less seen. As there is less air, said air will give less light to said shadow. Said shadow will be less seen because it will be less seen, and said air will give less light to said shadow. And said air will be so much clearer as the shadow is less seen by the eye; less light will be seen through said air. The appearances of colors vary in three ways.

Necessity of lights and bodies
Of seeing the lights
Proportionality of the lights
Light and shadow, one and the other
Proportionality of colors

### FOLIO 31 — recto. [N. 12]
->On spirits<-

<margin>The intimate union of the spirit with the body as a condition of its existence.</margin>
We have until now, behind this page, stated how the definition of the spirit is <note>original: "un nome non congiunto" - a name not joined to a physical thing</note> a power joined to the body, because by itself it cannot support itself, nor take on any kind of local motion <note>movement from one place to another</note>; and if you should say that it supports itself, this cannot be within the elements, because, if the spirit is an incorporeal quantity <note>a measurement without a physical body</note>, such a quantity is called a vacuum, and a vacuum does not exist in nature; and even if it did exist, it would immediately be filled by the collapse of that element in which such a vacuum was generated.

<margin>The concept of the weight of bodies. Consequences for the existence of the spirit.</margin>
Therefore, by the definition of weight, which says: gravity is an accidental power <note>a force that is not inherent but results from circumstances</note>, created by one element being drawn and pushed into another, it follows that no element has weight within that same element, but it has weight in the element above it, which is lighter than itself; as is seen, a portion of water has neither gravity nor lightness in other water, but if you draw it up into the air, then it will acquire weight <note>Leonardo is arguing that "spirits" cannot exist independently because they would create a vacuum, which nature abhors, and they lack the physical properties of the elements</note>.

### ON ANATOMY. — FOLIO B. — 31 RECTO.

...that it infuses itself into a quantity of air; and if it mixes with the air, two disadvantages follow: namely, that it <term>lightens</term><note>original: "levificha"; Leonardo means the spirit would reduce the density of the air it occupies.</note> that quantity of the air where it is mixed, for which reason the lightened air flies upward of its own accord and does not remain within the air that is thicker than itself. And besides this, such <term>spiritual power</term><note>original: "virtu spirituale"; in this context, the inherent force or essence that allows the spirit to function.</note>, once spread out, becomes disunited and alters its nature, for which reason it lacks its primary power. To this, a third disadvantage is added, and this is that such a body of air, taken up by the spirit, is subject to the penetration of the winds, which continually disunite and tear apart the joined parts of the air, rolling and swirling them through the other air. Therefore the spirit, infused in such ÷ [Continues at the top of Folio 30 *verso*, at the sign ÷] air, would be dismembered, or torn apart and broken, along with the tearing apart of the air in which it was infused.

<meta>This page begins a new section of anatomical observations, moving from the general structure of the body to specific studies of the musculature of the hip and the function of the gallbladder.</meta>

# ANATOMY — Sheets B. 31 — Recto

Of the muscles that move the thigh, there are three; and these originate from the bone of the pelvis <note>original: "bacino"</note> and go to join with the upper part of the thigh bone, between the joint of said thigh and the muscle called the pectineus <note>original: "pettine"; a flat, quadrangular muscle at the anterior part of the upper and medial aspect of the thigh</note>. And these such muscles go from the front part to the inner part, and they are arranged to pull the thigh inward toward the other thigh.

Of the muscles that pull the thigh outward toward the hips: these originate from the outer part of the pelvic bone and join with the outer part of the thigh bone, between the joint of said thigh and the muscle of the hip. And these are three muscles because one exceeds the other in strength; and this is done by Nature because if a man is loaded upon one shoulder, and the weight hangs outside the base of the foot that supports such weight, then the muscles of the hip are those that straighten the man. And the heavier the weight may be, the more of these muscles will be employed for such straightening <note>Leonardo is describing the biomechanics of balance and the role of the abductor muscles in stabilizing the pelvis during movement or weight-bearing</note>.

---

Of the gallbladder <note>original: "uesica del fiele"</note> and its channels, which are two: one is that which carries the bile from the liver to the bladder, and the other is that which carries said bile from the bladder to the stomach—or you might say to the beginning of the intestine called the duodenum. And this second channel is wider than the other, because the first has to give the bile drop by drop to the bladder, and the second has to fly <note>meaning to flow rapidly</note> more bile in the same amount of time when the stomach has need of being aided by the sharpness <note>original: "astutie," literally "shrewdness" or "cunning," here used metaphorically for the chemical potency or "acuteness" of the bile</note> of such bile, so that the food may be turned to ash <note>original: "s'incenerischi"; Leonardo uses the concept of "incineration" to describe the corrosive or transformative process of digestion</note> more quickly.

Of the channels of the bile: one enters the duodenum, and the other originates from the liver, and the third originates from the bladder; and they unite together and make themselves into one channel only, and this goes to fix itself inside the duodenum.

<summary>Leonardo describes the mechanical function of the hip muscles in maintaining balance while carrying loads, alongside a study of the gallbladder's biliary ducts and their role in digestion.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, myology, thigh muscles, biomechanics, gallbladder, bile ducts, digestion, duodenum, liver</keywords>

Of the muscles that move the thigh, there are three; and these originate from the pelvic bone <note>original: "bacino"</note> and go to join with the upper part of the thigh bone, between the joint of said thigh and the muscle called the **pectineus** <note>original: "pettine"; a flat, quadrangular muscle at the anterior part of the upper and medial aspect of the thigh</note>. <meta>This page transitions from the anatomical observations of the previous page to Leonardo’s investigations into optics and atmospheric physics. ### On Light

There are many who believe that the air is luminous in itself with a clear light,
and they say that if the air were not inherently luminous, the sun could not
illuminate the hemisphere <note>original: "lemisperio"; referring to the dome of the sky visible above the horizon</note> with a white light such as we see.
In their opinion, if the air were not luminous in itself, the shadows of the
night would be as black as pitch <note>original: "pece"; a thick, dark resin used for waterproofing ships, often used as a metaphor for absolute darkness</note> in the dark of a locked stable.
But the true reason is this: the air is not luminous in itself,
nor is it dark in itself, but it is of such a nature that it adopts every visual quality
that comes before it. And because the air is found between the
darkness of the shadows and the splendor of the sun, it appears as a
medium light <note>an intermediate or neutral light</note> as we see, because it is a mixture of
darkness and of light; and for this reason, we see it as white.
But truly, the whiteness that we see is not
the whiteness of a simple light, but is a composite whiteness
composed of light and of darkness.
And by this whiteness, we see things that are in the
shadows more than we would if such air were not
illuminated by a white light. And they say that if the air
were luminous in itself, there would not be such a difference
of light from one part <unclear>to</unclear> the other, nor would you have such great
notice of the light of the sun as we do, for the reason
that we see the sun's light to be, in truth, much
clearer than the light of the air. And if the air were in itself
luminous, we would not see such a difference.
And for this reason, we conclude that the air is not luminous in itself.

---

### On Light and Shadow

That point of the air which is closer to the center <note>original: "unita"; literally "unity," likely referring to the solar disk or the direct path of the sun's rays</note> of the sun
will be more luminous; and that which is further away will be less
luminous, because it will be more mixed with the darkness of the
black air <note>Leonardo often theorized that the "higher" atmosphere or space beyond the air was naturally black</note> that surrounds it. And that which is less luminous
will be more similar to darkness; and this will be the reason
that things placed in shadow are seen more or less
according to the quantity of light that illuminates them. And if the air
were luminous in itself, we would see things that are in the
shadows as white and of a uniform light, and such air would not create
shadows nor highlights on any object placed in said air.
But we see that things placed in shadow have
light and shadows with truth, with true relief <term>relief: "rilievo"; the quality of looking three-dimensional or standing out from the background in a painting</term>, which
would not happen if the air were luminous in itself, because
the light of the air would illuminate every part with
equal whiteness. And we see this in cloudy weather,
when things lack relief because they have no shadows;
and thus they are illuminated from every side because the clouds are like
the air of which we have spoken.

<summary>Leonardo argues that air is not inherently luminous but acts as a medium that reflects and mixes light and darkness. He explains that the sky's appearance and the visibility of objects in shadow are due to this atmospheric mixture, which is essential for creating the "relief" or three-dimensionality seen in nature and art.</summary>
<keywords>optics, light, shadow, atmospheric perspective, relief, sun, atmosphere, darkness, painting theory, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

# ANATOMY — Folio B. 31 — Verso.

skin of the mouth

The muscles that move the lips of the mouth are more numerous in man than in any other animal. And this reasoning is necessary for man because of the many <term>accidents <gloss>original: accidēti</gloss> <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to the various expressive movements or phonetic variations required for speech.</note></term> that speech demands, which are many more than the sounds of the mouths of other animals <unclear>~</unclear>

in which the members have among them as many various functions as there are various accidents of the various motions of said mouth and lips <unclear>~</unclear>

The lips have their own muscles and common muscles; those are "own" <note>intrinsic</note> which are internal to those same lips, of which one is visible and another is invisible; the "common" ones are those which go to terminate in the lips to pull them, and they originate outside of said lips <unclear>~</unclear>

Those which are intrinsic in the lips are 4, and these have their <term>cords <gloss>original: corde</gloss> <note>Leonardo uses "cords" to describe tendons or fibrous muscle attachments.</note></term> which go into the upper lip, specifically into the <term>corners <gloss>original: cātiti</gloss></term> of said mouth, and from there 2 others arise in the lower lip which similarly go to terminate in the corners of said mouth <unclear>~</unclear>

If it is possible that many muscles move together, or that some of them stay still, or that some are set in slow or fast motion by the various accidents of the soul <note>Leonardo often links physical facial expression directly to the "accidents of the soul," or emotions.</note> ~ then it will be necessary to see which muscles have a common cord which is maintained in suspension by a muscle that is stretched and maintained by another muscle <unclear>...</unclear>

The <term>pinnule <gloss>original: pēna</gloss> <note>Literally "feather" or "fin," here referring to a specific structural part of the muscle fibers.</note></term> of muscle **o** is that which maintains the 4 muscles **a b c d** in motion or in quiet with itself. The more the cord of one of these muscles is stretched, the more relaxed will be that of the other muscle, all of which are opposite on the same lip; and so it is with all the muscles of the face, which all have their origin or their end in the lips of said mouth ~

The nerve that gives sensation to the lips of the mouth is the same that also gives motion to their muscles, and it is that which arises from the seventh pair of cranial nerves <note>original: settimo paio de’ nerui del cieruello</note>, and this goes into the muscles of the lips, passing through the holes of the lower jaw <unclear>...</unclear>

which lips, if they were without their skin above and below, would open up due to the pulling of these muscles <unclear>...</unclear>

### FOLIO 32 — *verso*. [16]
### Of the old man <note>Leonardo frequently used the body of a centenarian he had dissected in Florence as his primary anatomical model.</note>

<margin>Precepts for the demonstration of the vessels of the neck, and their importance for life.</margin>
But make this demonstration from three different aspects, that is: from the front, from the side, and from behind.

[Fig. 145 :] m n S a b o c

If you compress the 4 veins *m* on each side where they are in the throat, the person whose veins are compressed will immediately fall to the ground sleeping, and as if dead, and will never wake up by himself; and if he is left in such a state for the hundredth part of an hour <note>original: "un centesimo d'ora"; Leonardo's way of describing a very brief duration, roughly 36 seconds.</note>, he will never wake again, neither by himself nor by the help of others.

*a* are ramifications of the artery.
*b* is the ramification of the veins.
*c* is the cephalic vein <term>cephalic vein: a superficial vein of the arm, which Leonardo here traces toward the neck</term>.
*n* are two veins that enter into the vertebrae <note>original: "isspondili"</note> of the neck to nourish them.
*o* is the basilic vein.
*S* are the apoplectic veins <note>original: "vene popletiche"; Leonardo refers to the jugular veins, so named because their compression was thought to cause "apoplexy" or stroke-like unconsciousness.</note>.

<note>This page (f. 4v) contains a celebrated passage where Leonardo da Vinci defends the necessity of botanical and anatomical illustration as a scientific tool superior to written description.</note>

<note>Leonardo’s mirror writing is transcribed here into standard English. He is addressing future anatomists or perhaps himself as a researcher.</note>

O you who, with such diligence, have
demonstrated the nature of man in your
judgment: restrain your
annoyance, and do not merely describe
the pathways of the veins with your 
pen, but identify them by name 
and through illustration. 
And do not describe them with words alone, 
because the eye captures more meaning
in seeing than the ear does in hearing.

<note>Leonardo argues for the "science of painting." In the Renaissance, many scholars believed text was the only way to convey complex truth; Leonardo countered that a single drawing could provide more immediate and accurate information than pages of prose.</note>

<margin>Trachea, esophagus, stomach.</margin>
How the rings <note>original: "anuli"</note> of the trachea do not join for two reasons; one is for the voice, and the other is to allow space for food between themselves and the bone of the neck <note>the cervical vertebrae of the spine</note>.

[Fig. 147.]

Of the old man.

Count the rings of the trachea.

[Fig. 148 :] a b n m f.

<margin>Vagus nerve and its function, and the varied structure of the brain.</margin>
Note in which part the left **recurrent nerve** <term>recurrent nerve: the recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus nerve that "loops" or reverses direction to reach the larynx</term> turns, and what purpose it serves.

And note the substance of the brain, whether it is thinner <note>rarer</note> or denser above the origin of the nerves than in its other parts; and see in what way the recurrent nerves provide sensation to the rings of the trachea, and which muscles are those that provide movement to these rings to produce a **deep, medium, and high-pitched voice.**

The recurrent nerves originate in *a b*, and *b f* is the recurrent nerve, descending to the porti— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely intended to be "portion" or "portal"</note>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

...descending to the <term>pylorus</term><note>original: "portinaro dello stomaco" - literally the 'doorkeeper' of the stomach</note> of the stomach; and the left nerve, companion to this one, descends to the casing of the heart, and I believe that this is the nerve that enters into the heart.

<margin>
The heart, a muscle nourished, like the others, by the artery and the vein.
</margin>
The heart in itself is not the principle of life; but it is a vessel made of dense muscle, vivified and nourished by the artery and vein, as are the other muscles. It is true that the blood and the artery, which is purified within it, are the life and nourishment of the other muscles; and it is of such density that fire can hardly harm it. This is seen in men who have been burned, whose bones have been turned to ash, yet the heart is still bloody inside. Nature has created such great resistance to heat so that it can withstand the great heat generated in the left side of the heart by means of the blood called "arterial," which becomes refined in that ventricle.

### Anatomy of the neck

The lungs cannot send away the air from between the <term>membranes</term><note>original: "lamine"; here referring to the pleural layers or the tissue of the lungs.</note> of said lung, if that membrane of the lung does not open in the same way that the leather sleeve of a **bellows** opens, providing a vent for the air that gathers within; rather, through that vent, it receives the air of the bellows into the cavity that fills it. And to determine if there is air inside the membranes of the lung, a test was made by inflating them through the vent of that lung and placing them under water to see if **bubbles** would emerge, and none came out. From this, it is concluded that the air of the lung does not pass through the aforementioned membranes; and this does not occur in either of the two ways: neither through the membranes nor through the blood vessels—those which go from the heart to the lung to <term>refresh</term><note>Leonardo follows the ancient theory that a primary function of breathing was to cool the "vital heat" generated by the heart.</note> the air received by said lung.

<margin>
<note>This text block is written on a separate fragment of paper pasted onto the left margin of the folio.</note>
Anatomy of the **vein** of said lung: and by this, it is demonstrated that it does not pass air, because even by inflating the lung very forcefully, no air bubble exited through that said vein. And likewise, regarding the **capillary veins** near the surface of the lung: if those were broken, inflating the lung and the escape of air would send bubbles under the water, and none appeared.
</margin>

Furthermore, one must gather the nerves that send motion to the muscles of the throat to make them shout, and gather those that send <term>sensation</term><note>original: "sentitiva"</note> to the linings of said muscles, to see which of them is interrupted first: the voice or the sensation of said muscles. And these nerves are those of the **sixth pair**<note>In the Galenic tradition Leonardo followed, the "sixth pair" of cranial nerves corresponds to what modern anatomy calls the Vagus nerve (the 10th cranial nerve).</note> which go toward the lung to refresh the heart; they are not those that receive the sensation of the heart, because none is apparent.

<note>Anatomical study of the esophagus, stomach, and respiratory tract. Leonardo is exploring whether air from the lungs enters the blood vessels or the pleural cavity, concluding it does not based on a water-immersion experiment.</note>

<margin>
**spinal cord**<note>original: "merolla"</note>
</margin>

<margin>
**trachea**
</margin>

<margin>
**rough artery**<note>original: "arteria aspera"; an archaic term for the trachea, so named because of the "rough" texture created by its cartilaginous rings.</note>
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo conducts a scientific experiment using water immersion to prove that lung tissue is airtight, concluding that air does not leak into the blood or pleural cavity. He also maps the "sixth pair" of nerves (vagus nerves) and their role in voice production and heart regulation.</summary>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

<margin>
Veins from the liver to the spleen, and their function.
</margin>

Regarding the two large veins that go from the liver to the spleen, which come from the major veins of the spine, I judge that they are collectors of the superfluous blood. This blood, being cleared out every day through the mesenteric veins <note>original: "vene mjserajce," the veins draining the intestines</note>, is deposited in the bowels. Once it has arrived there, it produces the same stench that one would find in the corpses within tombs, and this is the stench of the feces.

Of the old man <note>Referring to Leonardo's detailed dissection of a centenarian in Florence, c. 1506</note>.

[Fig. 153.]

The branching made by the umbilical cord, the vein, and the artery in the gate <note><term>porta</term>: the hilum or entrance of the liver</note> of the liver.

<margin>
Rules for the demonstration of the veins and arteries of the liver.
</margin>

First, illustrate all the branchings of the veins that come to the gate of the liver all together, and then each one by itself separately in 3 or 4 demonstrations; I said 3, because the vein and the artery follow the same path.

---

<margin>
Veins from the liver to the spleen, and their function.
</margin>

Regarding the two large veins, which go from the liver to the spleen, which come from the larger veins of the spine, I judge that they are collectors of the superfluous blood, which, by clearing it out every day through the mesenteric veins, is deposited in the bowels with the same stench—once it has reached them—that the whole would have in the dead in their graves, and this is the stench of the feces.

Of the old man.

[Fig. 153.]

Branching made by the umbilicus and the vein and the artery in the gate of the liver.

---

<margin>
Rules for the demonstration of the veins and arteries of the liver.
</margin>

First illustrate all the branchings of the veins, which come to the gate of the liver, all together, and then each one by itself separately in 3, or if you wish 4 demonstrations; I said 3, because the vein and the artery make the same journey.

<summary>Leonardo describes the drainage of "superfluous blood" from the liver and spleen into the intestines, attributing the odor of feces to this biological waste. He also provides instructions on how to scientifically illustrate the overlapping paths of hepatic veins and arteries.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, liver, spleen, mesenteric veins, portal vein, digestion, scientific illustration, dissection, vascular system</keywords>

### FOLIO 35 — recto.

<margin>
Olfactory nerves, optic nerves, and their relationships.
</margin>

*a, b, c, d* are the nerves that catch odors.
[Fig. 154 :] *c a b e n*
[Fig. 155 :] *a b e f c d*
The nerves originate from the outermost membrane <note>original: "panniculo ultimo," referring here to the meninges</note> that coats the brain and the nape.

*e, n* nerves are the optic nerves, which are located beneath the nerves called caruncles <note>Leonardo uses the term "caroncole" to describe the olfactory bulbs</note>; but the optic nerves serve the power of sight, and the caruncles the power of smell.

<margin>
Technique for the examination of the brain and the cranial nerves.
</margin>

You shall remove the substance of the brain as far as the borders of the *dura mater* <term>dura mater: the tough, outermost membrane enveloping the brain</term>, which is interposed between the cranial base <note>original: "osso basilare"</note> and the substance of the brain; then note all the locations where this *dura mater* penetrates the cranial base along with the nerves it coats, together with the *pia mater* <term>pia mater: the delicate innermost membrane enveloping the brain</term>. And you will acquire this knowledge with certainty when you diligently lift this *pia mater* little by little.

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

Little by little, beginning from the extremities and noting from part to part the location of the aforementioned perforations <note>original: "perforamẽtj"; likely referring to the openings or passages for vessels and nerves</note>, beginning first from the right or left side, illustrating that side entirely, and then you shall follow with the opposite side. This will provide you with knowledge of whether the preceding part was well-situated or not, and furthermore, it will make you understand if the right side is similar to the left side. And if you find it varied, review other dissections <note>original: "nathomje"</note> to see if such variation is universal in all men and women.

How the images of all objects pass through

<note>Anatomical sketch showing the pair of eyes and the crossing of the optic nerves (optic chiasm).</note>

<margin>
The fifth visible points are of less value and are straight.
</margin>

<note>Anatomical cross-section of the head showing the eyes, optic nerves, and the brain's ventricles, particularly the "sensus communis" (common sense).</note>

<margin>
The images <note>original: "spetie," referring to the visual species or likenesses of objects</note> of the objects penetrate through the opening of the pupil <note>original: "luce," literally 'light,' used here to mean the pupillary opening</note> and are imprinted upon the crystalline sphere <note>the lens</note>.
</margin>

All the images of the objects that come to the pupil enter through it and cross over one another upon the surface of the crystalline humor's <term>sferichità</term> <note>spherical shape or curvature</note>, where they are imprinted—and there they cross again—at the tip of the optic nerve—and from there they go to the <term>sēnso comūne</term> <note>the "common sense," a central faculty in the brain where Leonardo believed all sensory data was processed and judged</note>.

If the crystalline humor were not spherical, one would not be able to see except in a straight line; but because of its sphericity, as much as it receives through the pupil, so much it sends to the optic nerve.

By a straight line, vision does not see except for objects the size of the pupil; but the sphericity of the crystalline humor—which is of an immoderate size compared to the pupil—ensures that it receives everything the pupil sees.

<note>Detailed diagram of a single eye illustrating the passage of visual information through the pupil and lens to the optic nerve.</note>

<margin>
One cannot see without the optic nerve, and therefore such a nerve is <term>chavo</term> <note>hollow; Leonardo followed the ancient belief that nerves were tubes for the passage of "animal spirits"</note>.
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo explains the optical process of vision, arguing that the spherical shape of the lens allows the eye to capture a wide field of view and transmit it through the optic nerve to the brain's central processing center.</summary>
<keywords>optics, anatomy of the eye, crystalline lens, optic nerve, common sense, visual perception, neuroanatomy</keywords>

# How the images of all objects pass through

<note>Anatomical sketch showing the pair of eyes and the crossing of the optic nerves, known today as the optic chiasm.</note>

<margin>
The five visible points are of less value and follow a straight path.
</margin>

<note>Anatomical cross-section of the human head showing the eyes, the optic nerves, and the ventricles of the brain, with a focus on the "common sense" (sensus communis).</note>

<margin>
The images <note>original: "spetie," referring to the visual "species" or the formal likenesses of objects emitted into the air</note> of the objects penetrate through the opening of the pupil <note>original: "luce," literally "light," used by Leonardo here to denote the pupillary opening</note> and are imprinted upon the crystalline sphere <note>the lens</note>.
</margin>

All the images of the objects that come to the pupil enter through it and cross over one another upon the surface of the crystalline humor's **spherical curvature** <term>sphericity</term> <note>original: sferichità; referring to the curvature of the lens</note>, where they are imprinted—and there they cross again—at the tip of the optic nerve—and from there they go to the **common sense** <term>sēnso comūne</term> <note>The "common sense" was a central faculty in Renaissance psychology, believed to be a physical location in the brain where all sensory data (sight, sound, etc.) was collected, compared, and judged.</note>.

If the crystalline humor were not spherical, one would not be able to see except in a straight line; but because of its sphericity, as much as it receives through the pupil, so much it sends to the optic nerve.

By a straight line, vision does not see except for objects the size of the pupil; but the sphericity of the crystalline humor—which is of a disproportionate size compared to the pupil—ensures that it receives everything the pupil sees.

<note>Detailed diagram of a single eye illustrating the path of light rays as they enter the pupil, refract through the lens, and converge toward the optic nerve.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains his theory of vision, proposing that images cross twice—once at the lens and once at the optic nerve—before being processed by the brain's "common sense." He emphasizes that the spherical shape of the lens is essential for a wide field of view.</summary>
<keywords>optics, anatomy of the eye, crystalline lens, optic nerve, common sense, light refraction, pupil, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

<margin>Preparation of the hemorrhoidal veins.</margin>
[Fig. 158.]
Cut the subject <note>The "subject" refers to the cadaver being dissected.</note> through the middle of the spine; but first tie off the chyle <note>The milky fluid containing fat droplets, drained from the lacteals of the small intestine during digestion.</note> and the artery so that they do not leak; and in this way, you will be able to see the hemorrhoidal veins halved, that is, in each division of the said subject.

[Fig. 159.]
Of the nourishment produced by putrefaction.

<margin>Mechanism of the formation of waste products in the intestine.</margin>
I say that the extremities of the mesenteric veins <note>original: "vene mjseraice"; these are the veins that drain blood from the intestines.</note>, which attract to themselves the substance of the food contained within the intestines, are dilated by means of the natural heat of man, because heat scatters and expands, while cold gathers and constricts. But this would not be sufficient if to that heat there were not added the stench produced by the corruption of the blood sent back from the arteries into those intestines. This blood acts within the intestines no differently than it does in burial tombs; this stench expands the viscera, penetrates all the pores, and thickens and swells the—

<summary>Leonardo describes a method for dissecting the spine to observe the hemorrhoidal veins and theorizes that intestinal expansion is caused by a combination of natural body heat and the "stench" of decomposing blood.</summary>

->### Entry of the urine into the bladder.<-

<margin>How the urine collects in the bladder passing through the ureters.</margin>

The urine, having departed from the kidneys, enters into the urinary pores <note>original: "poli oritidi"; referring to the ureters</note>, and from those it passes into the bladder near the middle of its height; and it enters into it through small perforations made transversally between tunic and tunic <note>Leonardo is describing the intramural course of the ureter through the layers or "tunics" of the bladder wall.</note>. # ANATOMY — Folio B. 37 — Recto.

<note>The following text is translated from Leonardo's mirror-image handwriting. He often used "mirror-writing" to prevent smudging ink as a left-handed writer, or perhaps to keep his notes private.</note>

<note>Anatomical diagrams of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder, illustrating internal structure and vascularization. The sketches explore the mechanism of the ureterovesical junction and the nature of the urethra.</note>

->**On the bladder**<-

The bladder is placed between the pubic bone <note>original: "osso del pettine," literally the "comb bone," an old anatomical term for the pubis</note> and the end of the intestine called the rectum <note>original: "monicholo," a term used in the Renaissance for the terminal part of the large intestine</note>, and above the root of the penis; and the urine that it receives enters through two urinary passages <note>the ureters</note>, which originate from the spine, that is, from the kidneys; and these are embedded in the passages that incline toward the center of the said bladder, and they have between one and the other skin <note>layers or tunics</note> of this bladder certain little flaps <note>original: "chappuccetti," literally "little hoods" or valves</note>, which close the hole where the said urine enters, so that because of the fullness of this bladder, that urine does not flow backward.

->**On the bladder**<-

No animal can live that has a wounded bladder, unless it were that a cancer or other disease corroded the skin of said bladder little by little, in such a way that nature, while one skin is destroyed, replaces it with another.

->**On the bladder**<-

That part of the urinary passage <note>the urethra</note> which goes from the neck of the bladder to the end of the penis, increases and decreases in length and thickness; it increases and decreases with the other parts of the penis, but it is not of the same substance as the penis, nor of the skin of the bladder, but is of the nature of a hollow and muscular nerve <note>term: "nerve" - in Leonardo's time, this could refer to any white, fibrous tissue including tendons or ligaments</note>, which can extend and retract; and such a substance is necessary, because if it were hard, it would break during the elongations of the penis, and if it were of a substance that could only dilate, it would not return to its original state.

<margin>
The bladder joins with the spine between the fifth and sixth vertebrae <note>original: "spondilo"</note>, counting from the end of the sacrum <note>original: "sasso della schina," literally "stone of the spine"</note>; this bladder is composed of two skins; one is separated from the other at the urinary passages, and there it creates a certain barrier, which, closing itself by the weight of the urine, does not let it flow backward.
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo describes the anatomical position of the bladder and the function of the ureteric valves ("chappuccetti") in preventing the reflux of urine. He also analyzes the material properties of the urethra, noting its ability to stretch and contract during changes in the state of the penis.</summary>

# On the bladder, the kidneys, and the urinary passages.

<note>Anatomical study of the urinary system, specifically the kidneys, ureters, and bladder. Leonardo investigates the relative positioning of the kidneys and the valvular mechanism of the ureters' entry into the bladder wall to prevent backflow.</note>

<margin>
On the position of the kidneys
</margin>

<note>Labels written below the three upper anatomical drawings in mirror script. These refer to the traditional Aristotelian and Galenic divisions of the soul:</note>
-> Sensitive soul <-
<note>original: "Anima sensitiva" — responsible for perception and movement.</note>
-> Vegetative soul <-
<note>original: "Anima vegetativa" — responsible for basic life functions like growth and nutrition.</note>
-> Rational soul <-
<note>original: "Anima rationale" — responsible for thought and reason.</note>

The kidneys are positioned such that one is lower than the other, and this is to give space to the liver which is on the right side, and the spleen which is on the left; if the kidneys were at the same level, either the spleen or the liver would be obstructed. But the kidneys are placed as high as is required so as not to give any hindrance to the said liver and spleen.

The <term>urinary passages: known today as the ureters</term> that go from the kidneys to the bladder pass through the said kidneys and go inside until almost the membrane of the bladder itself, and then they push between that membrane and the thin skin that covers it. When the bladder is full, then the urine or whatever air is there presses one layer of skin against the other, and thus the said passages are closed so that the urine cannot flow backward.

The urine is separated from the blood in the kidneys by the intent of nature, which, wishing to purify the blood of the surplus of water, sends it through the said passages to the bladder, and there it is collected.

If the bladder were full of air or wind, the urine would not be able to enter it; and lacking the will for it to exit, that urine could not leave the bladder.

<margin>
bladder
</margin>

<margin>
Why the urine that comes from the kidneys to the bladder does not return to the kidneys when the bladder is full of wind or anything else. It was ordained by nature that the said passages enter between the internal and external membranes of the bladder for the space of an inch; and when the bladder is empty, the urine enters through the said passages, and when it is full of wind or urine, these two veils close together and forbid the entry of that urine or any other air.
</margin>

<note>The small diagram at the bottom left, labeled 'a' (ureter) and 'b' (bladder wall), demonstrates the oblique passage of the ureter through the bladder wall, which creates a natural valve effect.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains the asymmetrical placement of the kidneys to accommodate the liver and spleen and provides a detailed mechanical explanation of how the ureters act as one-way valves into the bladder. He integrates these anatomical observations with the philosophical concept of the three souls (sensitive, vegetative, and rational).</summary>

# On the bladder, the kidneys, and the urinary passages.

<note>This page contains an anatomical study of the urinary system, specifically focusing on the kidneys, ureters, and bladder. Leonardo investigates the relative positioning of the kidneys and the clever valvular mechanism where the ureters enter the bladder wall, designed to prevent the backflow of liquid.</note>

<margin>
On the position of the kidneys
</margin>

<note>The following labels were originally written in mirror script beneath three anatomical drawings. They refer to the traditional Aristotelian and Galenic divisions of the soul, which Leonardo used to categorize biological and mental functions:</note>

-> Sensitive soul <-
<note>original: "Anima sensitiva" — The faculty responsible for sensory perception and movement.</note>

-> Vegetative soul <-
<note>original: "Anima vegetativa" — The faculty responsible for basic life functions such as growth and nutrition.</note>

-> Rational soul <-
<note>original: "Anima rationale" — The highest faculty, responsible for thought and reason.</note>

The kidneys are positioned such that one sits lower than the other. This arrangement is designed to provide sufficient space for the liver, which is located on the right side, and the spleen, which is on the left. If the kidneys were placed at the same level, either the spleen or the liver would be obstructed. Instead, the kidneys are situated exactly as high as required so they do not hinder these other organs.

The <term>urinary passages<note>Leonardo refers to these as "meati uritidi," known in modern medicine as the ureters.</note></term> that travel from the kidneys to the bladder pass through the kidneys and extend inward almost to the membrane of the bladder itself. From there, they pass between that membrane and the thin skin that covers it. When the bladder is full, the pressure from the urine (or any trapped air) presses one layer of tissue against the other. This action effectively closes the passages, acting like a one-way valve to ensure that urine cannot flow backward toward the kidneys.

# ANATOMY — FOLIO B. 37 — VERSO

<note>The following text is translated from Leonardo da Vinci's mirror script. The handwriting in this section is particularly delicate and faint.</note>

165
</margin>

<note>Drawing 165: A detailed anatomical study showing the larynx, the trachea, and the complex branching of the bronchial tubes and blood vessels within the lungs.</note>

The <term>trachea</term> <note>original: "asprezza dell’arteria", literally 'the roughness of the artery', a common Renaissance term for the windpipe due to its cartilaginous rings</note> is enclosed below by the lung, and above it is free and naked of any other covering.

->Channel of the pulmonary vessel.<-

These blood veins that branch through the lung together with the branchings of the trachea are veins through which the lung receives nourishment from that pulmonary vessel. And they are not veins with which the lung itself is nourished by blood. Because such nourishment through veins is performed by the <term>vena cava</term> <note>the large vein that returns blood to the heart; Leonardo is exploring how different vessels serve different functional or nutritional roles</note>.

<margin>
164
</margin>

<note>Drawing 164: A lateral view of the chest cavity, illustrating the physical connection between the heart, the trachea, and the lungs.</note>

The trachea, in its branching, always has a vein and an artery accompanying it; and this occurs because such branching of the trachea is made to provide air to those veins and arteries. But the vena cava does not accompany them in its branching.

It is seen how the heart is joined with the lung by the pulmonary vein and artery, and how the trachea is joined with the lung. And how the trachea is joined with the heart.

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

[Fig. 168.]

Just as the fingers of the hand interweave with one another in the spaces between them while remaining straight and facing each other, so do the fibers of the flesh of these **small sponges** <note>original: "spugnole"; Leonardo’s term for the cotyledons, the functional units of the placenta in ruminants</note> interweave, like **burrs** <note>original: "lappole"; referring to the hooked seeds of the burdock plant that cling to fur or clothing</note>, one half with the other.

[Fig. 169.]

As the small sponges, which join together the membranes <term>panniculi: thin layers of tissue or membranes</term> in the middle between the two ends, go about detaching one half from the other; one half goes away with the **offspring** <note>original: "figliol"; here referring to the calf fetus</note> when it is born "clothed" <note>born within the fetal membranes or amniotic sac</note>—that is, the half which is below—and the other half, which remains above, stays with the **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note>. These, being sown six by six, when the womb contracts, all these fleshy sponges come to touch each other with their sides, and finally join together with **hexagonal** sides; eventually they unite and become a single piece of flesh, which then again divide and spread out in the subsequent pregnancy.

[Fig. 170.]

<column-break/>

[Fig. 168.]

Just as the fingers of the hand interweave, one in the spaces of the others, while remaining straight and face-to-face, so do the threads of the flesh of these little sponges interweave, in the manner of burrs, one half with the other.

[Fig. 169.]

As the little sponges, which join together the membranes of the middle at the two extremities, go about detaching one half from the other, one half goes away with the **calf**, when it is born "clothed"—that is to say, the part that is underneath—and the other half, which is above, remains with the womb. These, being sown six by six, when the womb contracts, all these fleshy little sponges come to touch each other by their sides, and finally conjoin by hexagonal sides, and then unite, reducing themselves to a single piece of flesh; these then divide again and spread out in the successive fertilization.

[Fig. 170.]

**Anatomy, small sponges (cotyledons), womb, offspring/calf, pregnancy/fertilization, membranes, burrs, hexagonal.**

<summary>Leonardo describes the interlocking mechanism of the bovine placenta, comparing the way maternal and fetal tissues join to fingers of the hand or clinging burrs. He also observes how these tissues separate during birth and merge into a single mass as the uterus contracts afterward.</summary>

It can be seen here inside how the uterus is composed of a multitude of cotyledons, which are certain bonds that join the afterbirth with the body of the uterus; and these are so dense that the spaces between them are barely visible, and they are nothing other than vessels doubled one inside the other; these spaces arise and grow and <unclear>decrease</unclear> according to whether more or less blood passes through them.

The cow’s cotyledons are as thin as a doubled linen cloth, one inside the other, and they are so dense that the spaces between them are barely visible; they are nothing other than vessels doubled one inside the other, which spaces arise and grow and <unclear>decrease</unclear> according to whether more or less blood or nourishment for the animal passes through them; it is nourished through these vessels, which are inside other vessels, which are inside other vessels, and so on, step by step, until they reach the heart of the fetus.

[Fig. 180.]

The muscles called the lips of the mouth, when tightening toward their center, pull the lateral muscles along with them; and when the lateral muscles pull back into themselves, shortening <note>original: "raccordandosi"</note>, they then pull back the lips of the mouth, and in this way the mouth extends, etc.

The maximum shortening of the mouth becomes equal to half of its size when it is at its greatest extension; it is also equal to the maximum width of the nostrils of the nose and to the space between the tear ducts <gloss>na</gloss> of the eyes.

There are two movements that the lips make when they contract: the first is that which closes and presses one lip against the other; the second movement is that which contracts or shortens the width of the mouth. # LEONARDO DA VINCI

<note>This page contains a facsimile reproduction of Leonardo's manuscript, written in his characteristic mirror script—which reads from right to left—alongside anatomical sketches of the mouth and lips.</note>

<margin>.0219V -- 8</margin>
The skin that covers the muscles that pull <note>original: "vestitrice de li musscholi che tirano"</note> directs itself, with its wrinkles, toward the place where the cause of the motion is located; and according to the 5th rule of **ANATOMY**: <term>muscle power</term> <note>Leonardo explains that muscles function only through contraction, never by pushing.</note> never exerts its power by pushing, but always by pulling toward itself the parts joined to it. Therefore, the center of the muscles called the lips of the mouth pulls toward itself the ends of said mouth along with parts of the cheeks; and because of this, the mouth always fills with wrinkles when performing such a function.

---

The skin, covering the muscles that pull, directs itself with its wrinkles to the place where the cause of the movement resides; and by the 5th rule: no muscle employs its power in pushing, but always in pulling toward itself the parts joined to them; therefore, the middle of the muscles, called the lips of the mouth, pulls to itself the extremities of that mouth along with a part of the cheeks, and for this reason the mouth always fills with wrinkles in this function.

<note>The following section is a French translation of the Italian text above, here rendered into English for accessibility.</note>

This says: the skin, the envelope of the muscles that pull, always directs itself, with its wrinkles, to the place where the cause of the movement is; and by the 5th rule: no muscle uses its power to push, but always to pull to itself the parts which are joined to it; therefore, the middle of the muscles, called the lips of the mouth, pulls to itself the ends of this mouth with a part of the cheeks, and for that reason the mouth always fills with wrinkles during this function.

<note>The sketches on this page (numbered 134–140) illustrate these mechanical principles, showing the vertical folds in the skin when the lips are pursed and the tension in the cheeks when the mouth moves.</note>

# ON ANATOMY — FOLIO B — 40 RECTO

### FOLIO 40 — *recto*.

<margin>Sections of the skull.</margin>
[Fig. 182]
[Fig. 183 :] *r a c b h f n m*

<margin>Determining the location of the confluence of the senses.</margin>
Where the line *a m* intersects with the line *c b*, there shall be the confluence of all the senses <note>Leonardo is searching for the *sensus communis* (common sense), a traditional philosophical and anatomical concept of a central point in the brain where all sensory input—sight, hearing, touch, etc.—is processed together.</note>; and where the line *r n* intersects with the line *h f*, there shall be the pole of the skull, at one-third of the height of the head, and thus *c b* will be at the midpoint.

<margin>Instructions for the description of the skull.</margin>
Remember, when you illustrate this half-head from the inside, to make another that shows the outside, turned in the same direction as this one, so that the whole may be better understood <note>This demonstrates Leonardo’s sophisticated approach to technical illustration, emphasizing that internal and external views must be aligned to help the viewer spatialize the anatomy.</note>.

<summary>On this page, Leonardo applies geometric proportions to the human skull to locate the "confluence of the senses" and provides methodological notes on how to best illustrate anatomical structures from both internal and external perspectives.</summary>
<keywords>skull anatomy, sensus communis, anatomical geometry, brain research, scientific illustration, cranial proportions</keywords>

# ON ANATOMY — SHEETS B — 41 RECTO.

### FOLIO 41 — recto. [F.]

[Fig. 186:] *b a m n a m*

<margin>
Cranial cavity. Seat of the "confluence of all the senses" and its relationships.
</margin>

The confluence of all the senses <note>original: "concorso di tutti i sensi"; Leonardo is referring to the *sensus communis*, a theoretical central point in the brain where all sensory information was thought to be processed</note> has beneath it, in a perpendicular line, the uvula—where one tastes food—at a distance of 2 fingers. It is positioned directly above the windpipe <note>original: "canna del polmone"</note> and above the opening of the heart <note>original: "buso del core," likely referring to the cardiac orifice or the superior vessels</note> at a distance of one foot. Above it, at half a head's distance, lies the joint of the skull bone. In front of it, along a horizontal <term>hemispheric|referring to a line following the curve of the skull</term> line, are the tear ducts of the eyes at one-third of a head's distance. Behind it, it has the nape of the neck at two-thirds of a head's distance. On its sides are the two pulses of the temples, at equal distance and height. As for the veins that are depicted inside the skull, in their branching they imprint half of their thickness into the bone of the skull, while the other half is hidden within the membranes <term>meninges|the protective layers covering the brain</term> that clothe the brain. And where the bone is lacking in veins on the inside, it is compensated on the outside by the vein *a m*, which, having exited the skull, passes into the eye and then into the...

<margin>
Vessels of the <term>diploe|the spongy layer of bone between the inner and outer layers of the skull</term> and the cerebral meninges.
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo describes the geometric and proportional center of the skull, which he identifies as the "confluence of all senses," measuring its distance from various anatomical landmarks like the heart, uvula, and temples. # ANATOMY — SHEETS B

## 41 — Recto

->186<-

<note>This page displays a facsimile reproduction of an anatomical drawing by Leonardo da Vinci. It shows a sagittal section <term>sagittal section: a vertical plane that divides the body or an organ into right and left parts</term> of a human skull. Leonardo has drawn the skull as if it were transparent to reveal the internal structures, specifically the brain's ventricles <term>ventricles: the hollow cavities within the brain that Leonardo believed housed the "sensus communis" or common sense</term> and the cranial nerves. A diagonal line is drawn through the skull, indicating Leonardo's attempt to apply geometric and perspectival rules to locate the exact center of the head and the seat of the soul.</note>

<warning>Faint ghosting of text from the reverse side of the folio is visible in the lower half of the central plate area. This is bleed-through from the ink on the other side and should not be confused with the drawing on this page.</warning>

<note>original: "Anatomia, Fogli, Recto, cranio, ventricoli" — Anatomy, Sheets, Front, skull, ventricles.</note>

This study represents a significant moment in the history of science, where Leonardo moves beyond mere surface observation to explore the "functional geography" of the human head. By sectioning the skull, he sought to understand how sensory information was channeled into the brain.

<summary>This page features a pivotal anatomical study of the human skull by Leonardo da Vinci, using transparency and sectioning to map the internal cavities of the brain and the paths of the nerves.</summary>

<note>Anatomical study of a human skull, sectioned to show the interior of the cranium and the vascular patterns on the inner surface of the bone. Reference lines for coordinates intersect at the location believed to be the 'senso comune'.</note>

Where the line **a-m** meets the line **c-b**, there is the meeting point of all the senses; and there meets the vein of moisture from which the <term>spirits</term> <note>In Renaissance physiology, 'spirits' were considered subtle fluids or vapors that traveled through the nerves to transmit sensation and movement.</note> are generated. And in that place is found the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: 'senso chomune'; the theoretical central point in the brain where all five senses converge to be processed.</note>. The reason for it is hidden throughout the entire mass of the **brain**, which is surrounded by the **pia mater** and the **dura mater**.

The line **p-n** is the line below which is the function of that sac: **p** above and **n** below. Each spindle <note>original: 'fuso'; likely referring to the shape of the cranial cavities or ventricles.</note> is one-third the width of a brain. This is the function of the sac in which these spirits are enclosed, and these functional spaces are of equal length, width, and height.

This brain is surrounded by three <term>membranes</term> <note>original: 'pannichuli'</note>: the first is that which is seen inside, namely the **pia mater** <note>The delicate innermost membrane surrounding the brain.</note>; the second is that which encloses it, namely the **dura mater** <note>The tough outermost membrane.</note>; the third is the **bone of the head**, which bone surrounds the whole.

<summary>Leonardo identifies the "senso comune" (common sense) at the geometric center of the skull, where he believes sensory data and "vital spirits" converge. He also provides an early, accurate description of the brain's protective layers: the pia mater, dura mater, and the skull itself.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, skull, brain, common sense, senso comune, spirits, pia mater, dura mater, neurobiology, cranial membranes</keywords>

# On the 2nd day of April 1489, the book titled "On the Human Figure"

<note>Anatomical studies of the human skull. The top drawing shows a superior-oblique view of the cranium with focus on the sagittal and coronal sutures <note>the joints where the bones of the skull meet</note>. The lower drawing is a lateral study of the skull (left side), focusing on the orbits <note>eye sockets</note>, zygomatic bone <note>cheekbone</note>, and the maxilla/mandible <note>jaw</note> structure.</note>

I wish to section the head and, by means of straight lines, demonstrate the location of the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "senso comune"; a traditional Aristotelian concept Leonardo sought to locate physically, believed to be the place where all five senses meet in the brain</note>, and at what height one section is above the other, and the thickness of the head, and the bone of the jaw, and one tooth above the other. And of what thickness one tooth is above the other, and by a straight section there must be a tooth; and of what height one tooth is above the other, and of what thickness one tooth is above the other. And on the other side, these holes will show how the jaw and the bone of the teeth join with the bony structure of the head, and how the <term>common sense</term> is situated above the <term>nape</term> <note>original: "nucha"; here referring to the spinal marrow or the junction of the brain and spinal cord</note>.

<column-break/>
